## 6. AI/LLM Pipeline

**Models:** Claude Sonnet 4 (risk analysis, redlines, summary — $3/$15 per M tokens) and Claude Haiku 3.5 (classification — $0.80/$4). Anthropic SDK, `temperature=0`, structured output via **tool use** with strict Pydantic-validated JSON schemas. All calls traced in **Langfuse**. Prompt caching on the shared system prompt + playbook block (cache reads at $0.30/M cut input cost ~60%).

**Stage 0 — Parse.** Digital PDFs: PyMuPDF text extraction with block coordinates. Scanned/image PDFs (detected when text layer < 50 chars/page): Azure Document Intelligence `prebuilt-layout` (OCR + headings + reading order). DOCX: python-docx, walking paragraphs/styles. Output: normalized text + heading structure + page map.

**Stage 1 — Segment.** Heuristic splitter: regex on numbered headings (`^\d+(\.\d+)*\.?\s+[A-Z]`), ALL-CAPS section titles, recital markers; merge fragments < 200 chars into neighbors; split blocks > 2,000 tokens on paragraph boundaries. Produces `clauses` rows with char/page offsets.

**Stage 2 — Document metadata (1 Sonnet call).** Extract parties, contract type (MSA/NDA/SaaS/employment/other), effective date, term, and **defined terms dictionary** — fed into later prompts so redlines use correct defined terms.

**Stage 3 — Clause classification (Haiku, batched ~15 clauses/call).** Classify each clause into a 25-type taxonomy (indemnification, limitation_of_liability, termination, ip_assignment, confidentiality, data_protection, governing_law, assignment, non_solicit, payment_terms, warranty, force_majeure, auto_renewal, audit_rights, sla, insurance, dispute_resolution, notice, entire_agreement, amendment, survival, subcontracting, most_favored_customer, change_of_control, other). Output: `{clause_id, type, confidence}[]`.

**Stage 4 — Risk analysis (Sonnet, batched ~5 clauses/call).** System prompt embeds the org playbook rules for the detected clause types. For each clause: check against playbook (e.g., "liability cap < 12 months fees → high", "one-way indemnity → high", "unilateral amendment rights → critical"), detect missing standard protections, output `risk_level`, `risk_categories`, `explanation`, and a **mandatory `source_quote`** verbatim from the clause text — grounding guard against hallucination; analyses failing quote-validation are retried once then downgraded to `confidence < 0.5`.

**Stage 5 — Redlines (Sonnet, only medium/high/critical clauses).** Instructions: minimal-edit philosophy — preserve structure and defined terms, change only what the risk requires; output `suggested_text` (full replacement clause) + `rationale`. Perspective from `party_perspective` (default customer). Concurrency capped with `asyncio.Semaphore(5)`.

**Stage 6 — Missing clauses.** Compare detected types against expected set for the contract type (e.g., NDA must have confidentiality, term, exclusions, remedies); missing → findings in report.

**Stage 7 — Summary (1 Sonnet call).** Executive summary, top findings ranked by weighted score (critical=10, high=6, medium=3, low=1 → normalized 0–100 doc score), negotiation priorities.

**Reliability:** 3 retries with exponential backoff (tenacity) on 429/5xx, 90s timeout per call, per-document token/cost budget ($2 hard cap → abort with clear error), full pipeline idempotent (re-running a job upserts by clause ordinal). **Eval:** golden set of 5 annotated contracts; E2 runs classification/risk accuracy checks in Langfuse each evening; ship threshold ≥ 85% clause-type accuracy.

## 8. Observability, Logging, Error Handling

- **Error tracking:** Sentry — Python SDK (FastAPI integration) + Next.js SDK; separate DSNs per env; PII scrubbing enabled, **raw contract text never sent to Sentry** (only IDs and stage names). Alert on new issues + error-rate spike → Slack `#alerts`.
- **LLM observability:** **Langfuse** (cloud) — every LLM call traced with prompt, response, tokens, latency, cost, document_id tag; nightly eval run against golden set; per-stage cost dashboard.
- **Logging:** `structlog` JSON logs → Render log drain → **Better Stack (Logtail)**; correlation ID (document_id + job_id) on every log line. Log levels: never log clause text above DEBUG.
- **Uptime:** Better Stack synthetic checks on `/healthz` and `/login` every 60s; Slack + SMS on-call for the launch week.
- **Error handling contract:**
  - API: global exception handler → consistent `{error: {code, message}}`; 422 validation, 403 tenant/role, 404 scoped misses.
  - Pipeline: each stage wrapped; transient failures retry (3×, backoff); permanent failures set `documents.status=failed` with a human-readable `error` shown in UI + "Retry" button (re-enqueue is idempotent).
  - Dead letters: failed jobs land in RQ failed queue, surfaced in a minimal `/admin/jobs` page for the team.
  - LLM provider outage: circuit breaker (pybreaker) opens after 10 consecutive failures; queued jobs pause rather than burn retries; status banner in UI.
- **Audit:** all mutations (redline accept/edit, report export) write `audit_logs` rows.

## 10. Cost Estimate — 100 active users/month

**Usage assumptions:** 100 users × 15 contracts/month = **1,500 docs**, avg 15 pages / ~12k tokens, ~60 clauses each. Per-doc LLM usage ≈ 45k input (≈60% served from prompt cache) + 12k output, blended across Haiku (classification) and Sonnet (everything else).

| Item | Basis | Est. monthly |
|---|---|---|
| Anthropic Sonnet 4 (risk/redline/summary) | ~1,200 docs × heavy stages, cached inputs | $380–450 |
| Anthropic Haiku 3.5 (classification) | 1,500 docs × batched calls | $30–50 |
| Azure Document Intelligence | ~20% of 22.5k pages scanned → ~4.5k pages @ ~$10/1k; digital PDFs free via PyMuPDF | $45–60 |
| Render (2× web @ $25, 2× worker @ $25) | | $100 |
| Supabase Pro (Postgres + Auth + Storage) | | $25 |

| **Total** | | **≈ $725–890/month** |

**Unit economics:** ~$0.30–0.40 LLM + ~$0.03 parsing ≈ **$0.35–0.45 per contract reviewed**. At any reasonable B2B price point ($50–200/user/month) gross margin is > 85%. Costs scale roughly linearly with doc volume; prompt caching is the main lever.

## 11. Top 5 Technical Risks & Mitigations

1. **Parsing failures on messy/scanned PDFs** (tables, multi-column, scans) — the #1 silent killer of doc-AI demos. *Mitigation:* PyMuPDF-first with automatic Doc Intelligence OCR fallback triggered by low text-density detection; upload-time validation (page/size limits); a day-6 edge-case gauntlet with deliberately ugly contracts; clear "we couldn't parse page X" errors rather than silent garbage.
2. **LLM hallucination / unsound legal analysis** — fatal for credibility with lawyers. *Mitigation:* mandatory verbatim `source_quote` grounding with validation-and-retry; `temperature=0`; strict schema-validated outputs; confidence surfaced in UI; human-in-the-loop framing ("suggestions, not legal advice"); nightly golden-set evals with a ship gate of ≥85% clause-type accuracy; Sonnet (not Haiku) for anything users read as advice.
3. **Latency/cost blowout on long contracts** (100+ page MSAs). *Mitigation:* clause-level batching + `asyncio.Semaphore(5)` parallelism; prompt caching; Haiku for the cheap stage; per-document $2 cost cap and 200-page limit; async UX with SSE so a 4-minute review feels managed, not hung.
4. **Confidential data leakage** — contracts are among the most sensitive docs a company has. *Mitigation:* RLS + org-scoped queries (defense in depth); Anthropic commercial terms (no training on inputs); raw text excluded from Sentry/logs; encryption in transit (TLS everywhere) and at rest (Supabase default); audit log on every access/export; private storage buckets with presigned URLs only.
5. **Timeline slip / scope creep** — 7 days with 3 people has zero slack. *Mitigation:* pre-agreed descope order (section 9); daily merge-to-main with CI gate kills integration surprises early; no custom playbook editor, no billing, no integrations — anything new proposed mid-week goes to the backlog list, not the board.

Here's my initial read on this, plus what I need to know to design something that actually fits your team rather than a generic "Slack bot" that adds more noise.

## Likely root causes (pick one or more)

1. **Notification overload** — too many channels, too many @here/@channel pings, bots/CI alerts flooding channels, no thread discipline.
2. **Duplicate work** — no shared visibility into who's working on what, so two people pick up the same task, or someone doesn't know a task was already done and redoes it.
3. **Both, linked** — because notifications are so noisy, people miss the one message that would've told them "someone's already on this," so they start it themselves.

A few directions this could go, depending on the cause:

- **Digest/triage bot**: collects notifications, mutes low-priority channels, and delivers a filtered daily/hourly summary instead of real-time pings.
- **Task claim system**: lightweight "I'm on this" tagging (could live in Slack via a slash command, or in a connected tracker like Linear/Jira) so duplicate work becomes visible before it happens.
- **Status/standup automation**: async daily check-in bot that surfaces "what is everyone working on right now" so overlaps get caught early.
- **Channel/notification audit + rules**: sometimes the fix isn't a new tool but restructuring channels, muting defaults, and enforcing thread usage — a bot to enforce/report on this.

## Questions before I recommend a specific build

1. **Team size and structure** — how many people, and are you one team or several teams sharing channels?
2. **What's the actual pain point** — is it more "too many notifications drowning out important ones" or "we keep duplicating each other's work," or both equally?
3. **What tools do you already use for tasks** — Jira, Asana, Linear, Trello, a spreadsheet, or is Slack itself the task tracker?
4. **Where's the duplicate work coming from** — same task claimed by two people, redoing work already done, or answering the same question multiple times in different threads?
5. **Technical constraints** — do you have someone who can build/maintain a custom Slack app/bot, or do you need something off-the-shelf/no-code?
6. **Volume** — roughly how many messages/notifications per day are we talking about, and in how many channels?

Once I know these, I can spec out something concrete — architecture, whether it's a Slack app vs. a workflow change vs. a lightweight integration with your existing tracker.

# Drug Interaction Review

## 1. Warfarin + Ibuprofen

**Severity: Major**

**Mechanism (multi-factorial):**
- **Pharmacodynamic synergy** — NSAIDs inhibit platelet COX-1, impairing thromboxane A2-mediated platelet aggregation. Combined with warfarin's anticoagulant effect, this produces additive bleeding risk independent of any effect on INR.
- **GI mucosal injury** — Ibuprofen inhibits prostaglandin-mediated gastric mucosal protection, increasing risk of GI ulceration/bleeding — a site-specific risk that compounds systemic anticoagulation.
- **Protein binding displacement** — Ibuprofen is highly protein-bound (~99%) and can transiently displace warfarin from albumin, increasing free warfarin fraction. This effect is generally considered minor/transient in clinical significance compared to the mechanisms above, but is worth noting.
- Ibuprofen is *not* a potent CYP2C9 inhibitor (unlike some other NSAIDs or azole antifungals), so metabolic interaction via CYP2C9 is not the primary concern here.

**Recommended action:**
- Avoid chronic/scheduled NSAID use in a patient on warfarin if at all possible. This is one of the most common preventable causes of major GI bleeding in anticoagulated patients.
- If short-term/occasional use is unavoidable, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, consider concurrent PPI for gastroprotection, and counsel patient on bleeding signs (melena, easy bruising, hematuria).
- Preferred alternative: acetaminophen for osteoarthritis pain (minimal interaction with warfarin at standard doses, though very high chronic doses >2g/day have been associated with modest INR elevation via unclear mechanism — monitor INR if used regularly).
- If NSAID therapy is clinically necessary long-term, consider referral back to prescriber to discuss alternative anticoagulation strategy or NSAID avoidance entirely.

---

## 2. Warfarin + Lisinopril

**No clinically significant direct pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interaction between these two agents.**

I want to be precise here rather than force an interaction that isn't well-supported: ACE inhibitors do not meaningfully affect warfarin metabolism (no significant CYP2C9 involvement) or platelet function. Some tertiary references list this as a "minor" interaction based on isolated case reports of INR fluctuation, but the evidence is weak and mechanism unclear/speculative. I would not flag this as clinically actionable in routine practice.

**Recommended action:** No specific action needed beyond routine INR monitoring already indicated for warfarin therapy.

---

## 3. Ibuprofen + Lisinopril

**Severity: Moderate**

**Mechanism:**
- NSAIDs inhibit renal prostaglandin synthesis (particularly PGE2 and PGI2), which normally maintain afferent arteriolar vasodilation in the kidney, especially under conditions of reduced renal perfusion. This prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation partially offsets ACE inhibitor-induced reduction in angiotensin II (which normally constricts the efferent arteriole to maintain GFR).
- Concurrent use can blunt the antihypertensive effect of lisinopril (via sodium/fluid retention and vasoconstriction) and increase risk of acute kidney injury, particularly in volume-depleted, elderly, or renally impaired patients ("triple whammy" concern if a diuretic were also added).
- There is also a modest additive hyperkalemia risk — ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone-mediated potassium excretion; NSAIDs can further reduce renal potassium excretion via reduced renin/aldosterone stimulation from decreased prostaglandins.

**Recommended action:**
- Use ibuprofen at the lowest effective dose, short duration, avoid regular scheduled dosing if possible.
- Monitor blood pressure control (efficacy of lisinopril may be reduced).
- Monitor renal function (BUN/creatinine) and serum potassium if NSAID use is more than occasional, particularly in older adults or anyone with baseline renal impairment or volume depletion.
- Ensure adequate hydration; use particular caution if patient is also on a diuretic (not listed here, but worth confirming it's not part of the full regimen).

---

## Summary / Priority Concern

The **warfarin–ibuprofen combination is the most clinically urgent issue** on this list given the major bleeding risk. Given that ibuprofen is prescribed PRN for osteoarthritis, I'd recommend discussing with the prescriber whether acetaminophen (± topical NSAID, which has much lower systemic absorption and interaction risk) could replace oral ibuprofen entirely, rather than trying to manage the interaction through monitoring alone. The lisinopril–ibuprofen renal interaction is a secondary but real concern, particularly if NSAID use becomes frequent.

# ICH E6(R2) Regulatory Analysis: Monitoring Approach and Informed Consent

## Question 1: Centralized-Only Monitoring

### Requirement
**Yes, ICH E6(R2) permits centralized-only monitoring, but with an important qualifier: it must be "justified."** This represents one of the most significant changes introduced by the R2 addendum (2016), which moved away from the presumption of mandatory on-site visits found in earlier guidance and industry practice.

### Relevant Citations

**Section 5.18.3 (Extent and Nature of Monitoring)** — as amended by the R2 addendum — states that the sponsor should develop a monitoring approach based on a systematic, prioritized, risk-based methodology. It explicitly identifies three permissible models:
- On-site monitoring only
- A combination of on-site and centralized monitoring
- **Centralized monitoring alone, "where justified"**

**Section 5.0 (Quality Management)**, added by R2, provides the underlying framework requiring sponsors to implement a quality management system that identifies critical data/processes and manages risk throughout the trial — this is the analytical basis that would justify a centralized-only approach.

**Section 5.18.4 (Monitor's Responsibilities)** lists the substantive verification activities a monitor must perform, regardless of the monitoring model chosen, including:
- Verifying informed consent was obtained appropriately (5.18.4(c))
- Verifying investigational product is stored, dispensed, and accounted for per protocol (5.18.4(d))
- Verifying source data/source documents and other trial records are accurate, complete, and consistent with source documents (5.18.4(e))
- Checking protocol adherence (5.18.4(f))
- Determining whether all AEs/SAEs are reported per requirements (5.18.4(n))

### Exceptions/Conditions
1. **"Where justified" is the operative caveat.** ICH E6(R2) does not treat centralized-only monitoring as a default acceptable option — the sponsor's monitoring plan must document the risk assessment supporting why remote/centralized methods are sufficient to fulfill the Section 5.18.4 responsibilities for this specific trial.
2. **Practical limitations for Phase III oncology trials specifically:** Certain verification activities are difficult to fully replicate centrally — e.g., verifying the informed consent process was conducted appropriately (not just that a signed form exists), physical drug accountability/storage conditions, and source document verification for complex oncology endpoints (imaging-based response assessments, adverse event grading tied to source records). Regulators (FDA's 2013 Guidance for Industry on risk-based monitoring, and EMA reflection papers) have generally expected a **combination approach** for complex, high-risk trials like Phase III oncology studies, with centralized monitoring supplementing rather than fully replacing on-site presence — though this is guidance-level expectation rather than an absolute E6(R2) prohibition.
3. Verify the specific numbering above against the current ICH E6(R2) consolidated guideline text, as I am recalling section structure from memory and pagination/lettering can vary slightly between the addendum document and integrated versions.

---

## Question 2: Investigator's Responsibilities for Informed Consent

### Requirement
The investigator bears direct, non-delegable ultimate responsibility for ensuring that informed consent is obtained properly from each subject (or their legally acceptable representative) before any trial-related procedures are performed, and that the process meets both ethical and procedural standards.

### Relevant Citations — Section 4.8 (Informed Consent of Trial Subjects)

Key sub-sections include:
- **4.8.1**: Informed consent must be obtained in accordance with GCP, the Declaration of Helsinki principles, and applicable regulatory requirements. The consent form and any written information must be approved by the IRB/IEC in advance, and revised whenever new information becomes available that may affect the subject's willingness to continue.
- **4.8.5**: Neither the investigator nor trial staff should coerce or unduly influence a subject to participate.
- **4.8.6**: Information must be provided in non-technical, understandable language.
- **4.8.7**: The subject must be given adequate time and opportunity to inquire about details of the trial before agreeing to participate.
- **4.8.8**: All questions should be answered satisfactorily.
- **4.8.10**: Prior to participation, the consent form must be signed and personally dated by the subject (or representative) **and by the person who conducted the informed consent discussion**.
- **4.8.11**: Where a subject is unable to read, an impartial witness must be present through the entire consent discussion, and the written information/consent form must be read and explained to the subject in the witness's presence.
- **4.8.14–4.8.15**: Lists specific required elements of the informed consent discussion (purpose, procedures, risks/benefits, alternatives, confidentiality, compensation, voluntary nature, right to withdraw, contact persons, etc.).

### Exceptions/Conditions
1. **Delegation**: The investigator may delegate the actual consent discussion to a qualified designee, but retains overall responsibility for ensuring the process was conducted properly and in compliance with 4.8 (this authority typically stems from Section 4.1, Investigator's Qualifications and Agreements, particularly 4.1.5 on delegation of trial-related duties).
2. **Emergency/Incapacitated subjects**: Section 4.8.15 addresses situations where prior written consent is not possible (e.g., emergency treatment), noting that consent of a legally acceptable representative should be obtained if possible, and that procedures should be described in the protocol with IRB/IEC approval.
3. **Vulnerable populations**: E6(R2) requires special attention/justification when enrolling vulnerable subjects (referenced in Section 3.1.8 regarding IRB/IEC review, and reinforced throughout 4.8).

Given this is a Phase III oncology trial, the informed consent process typically warrants heightened scrutiny given disease severity, treatment risks, and potential for therapeutic misconception — the monitor's verification of this process (per 5.18.4(c) above) is one of the more monitoring-intensive checks even under a risk-based approach, which is relevant to the centralized-monitoring justification in Question 1.

# AI Contract Review Assistant — 7-Day MVP Build Plan

## 1. System Architecture

**Components:**
- **Frontend SPA** (React) — hosted on Vercel, talks to backend via REST + polling
- **Backend API** (FastAPI, Python) — auth, CRUD, orchestration, hosted on Render
- **Worker service** (Celery + Redis broker) — async document processing pipeline, separate process from API
- **PostgreSQL** (Neon, with pgvector extension) — relational data + embeddings for clause similarity
- **Object storage** (AWS S3) — raw uploaded files, generated reports
- **LLM provider** (OpenAI API, GPT-4o-mini + GPT-4o) — extraction, classification, redline generation
- **Redis** — job queue broker + short-lived caching
- **Email** (Postmark) — transactional notifications
- **Sentry** — error tracking (frontend + backend)

**Data flow:**
1. User uploads PDF/DOCX → frontend requests presigned S3 URL from backend → uploads directly to S3.
2. Frontend calls `POST /contracts` with the S3 key → backend creates `contracts` row (status=`queued`), enqueues a Celery job.
3. Worker: downloads file → extracts text (PyMuPDF for PDF, python-docx for DOCX; OCR fallback via AWS Textract if text density is low) → segments into clauses (regex heuristics + LLM fallback for ambiguous blocks) → writes `clauses` rows.
4. Worker: for each clause, calls LLM to classify type → writes `clause_type`, confidence.
5. Worker: for each clause, runs playbook rule checks (deterministic) + LLM risk scoring → writes `risk_flags`.
6. Worker: for medium/high risk clauses, calls LLM (higher-capability model) to generate `redlines` (suggested text + rationale).
7. Worker marks contract `status=processed`; frontend polls `GET /contracts/{id}/status` (or short-poll every 3s) until done.
8. User reviews clauses/risks/redlines in the UI, accepts/rejects/edits.
9. User triggers `POST /contracts/{id}/report` → backend aggregates data → renders PDF (WeasyPrint) → stores in S3 → returns download URL.

## 4. Authentication & Authorization

- **JWT-based**: FastAPI + `python-jose` + `passlib[bcrypt]`. Access token (15 min TTL) in memory/header, refresh token (7 days) in httpOnly Secure cookie.

- **RBAC**: three roles — `admin` (manage users, playbook rules, billing), `reviewer` (upload, review, accept/reject redlines), `viewer` (read-only). Enforced via FastAPI dependency `require_role(["admin","reviewer"])`.
- **Password reset**: token via Postmark email link.
- Time-permitting alternative: swap custom JWT for Clerk/Auth0 to save ~half a day — noted as a Day 1 fork decision, but plan assumes custom JWT for full control over multi-tenant claims.

## 6. AI/LLM Pipeline

**Step 1 — Parsing:**
- PDF: PyMuPDF (`fitz`) for text + page/position metadata. If text density per page is below a threshold → route to AWS Textract OCR.
- DOCX: `python-docx`, walking paragraphs/headings to preserve structure.

**Step 2 — Clause segmentation:**
- Primary: regex/heuristics on numbered headings (`\d+\.`, `Section \d+`, `ARTICLE [IVX]+`, all-caps headers).
- Fallback: for blocks that don't match patterns, one LLM call (GPT-4o-mini, JSON mode) per document section asking it to return clause boundaries as structured JSON.

**Step 3 — Clause classification:**
- GPT-4o-mini, function-calling/JSON schema output, per-clause (batched in parallel with `asyncio` + semaphore for rate limiting).
- Taxonomy: indemnification, limitation_of_liability, termination, confidentiality, IP_assignment, governing_law, force_majeure, payment_terms, warranty, non_compete, assignment, dispute_resolution, data_protection, insurance, other.
- Output includes `confidence_score`; low-confidence clauses flagged for manual review in UI.

**Step 4 — Risk classification:**
- Deterministic layer: playbook rules (regex/keyword checks, e.g. "shall not be liable" without a cap → flag).
- LLM layer: GPT-4o-mini given clause text + clause type + matched playbook rule (if any, retrieved via pgvector similarity search on clause embeddings) → returns `risk_level`, `risk_category`, `rationale`. Few-shot examples embedded in the prompt for consistency.

**Step 5 — Redline generation:**
- Only run for medium/high risk clauses (cost control).
- GPT-4o (higher capability) given clause text + org's `standard_language` from matching playbook rule → returns `suggested_text` + `explanation`.

**Step 6 — Report generation:**
- Aggregate risk counts, list top flagged clauses, render via Jinja2 HTML template → WeasyPrint → PDF, uploaded to S3.

**Reliability:** Pydantic schema validation on every LLM JSON response; `tenacity` retry with exponential backoff (3 attempts) on malformed output or API errors; all calls logged to `llm_call_logs` for cost/latency tracking.

## 11. Top 5 Technical Risks & Mitigations

1. **LLM output inconsistency/hallucinated redlines.** Mitigation: strict JSON-schema/function-calling outputs, Pydantic validation with retry-on-invalid, few-shot prompting, confidence scores surfaced in UI, mandatory human review before any redline is applied — nothing auto-applies.

2. **Parsing failures on scanned/malformed contracts.** Mitigation: detect low text-density PDFs and auto-route to AWS Textract OCR; surface a clear "parsing may be imperfect" warning; allow manual clause boundary editing as fallback; test against diverse real templates starting Day 1.

3. **LLM cost/latency spikes on large contracts or concurrent uploads.** Mitigation: token-budgeted chunking, worker concurrency limits with semaphores, cheap model for extraction/classification and expensive model reserved only for flagged-clause redlines, per-org monthly usage caps, embedding-based caching to skip re-analyzing repeated boilerplate.

4. **Confidentiality/trust concerns from legal-team buyers uploading sensitive contracts.** Mitigation: encryption at rest (S3 SSE, Postgres) and in transit (TLS), use OpenAI API terms excluding data from model training, strict org-level isolation, audit logging, clear privacy policy/DPA even at MVP stage, SOC 2 noted as post-MVP roadmap item.

5. **Multi-tenancy bugs causing cross-org data leakage.** Mitigation: single shared query-scoping dependency used everywhere (no raw unscoped queries permitted), Postgres row-level security as defense-in-depth, dedicated integration tests asserting isolation, code-review checklist requirement for any endpoint touching contract data.

As a clinical pharmacist, here is the drug-drug interaction review for the patient's medication list:

---

### Interaction 1

1. **Interacting Drug Pair:** Warfarin + Ibuprofen
2. **Severity Classification:** Major
3. **Pharmacological Mechanism:**
   * **Pharmacodynamic synergy:** Ibuprofen inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), preventing the synthesis of thromboxane $\text{A}_2$ and resulting in reversible platelet inhibition. Concurrently, ibuprofen causes gastric mucosal injury by suppressing gastroprotective prostaglandins ($\text{PGE}_2$). Combined with warfarin’s inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), which depletes factors II, VII, IX, and X, this drastically amplifies the risk of severe upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
   * **Pharmacokinetic contribution:** Ibuprofen can competitively inhibit CYP2C9 (the enzyme primary responsible for metabolizing the more potent S-enantiomer of warfarin) and displace warfarin from plasma albumin binding sites, which can transiently increase free warfarin concentrations.
4. **Recommended Clinical Action:** Discontinue scheduled/PRN oral ibuprofen. Recommend an alternative analgesic with a lower bleeding profile, such as acetaminophen (monitored and limited to $\le 2\text{ g/day}$ for chronic use) or topical NSAIDs (e.g., diclofenac gel). If systemic NSAID therapy is strictly necessary, co-prescribe a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) for gastroprotection, use the lowest effective NSAID dose for the shortest duration, and monitor the patient's INR and signs of bleeding closely.

---

### Interaction 2

1. **Interacting Drug Pair:** Ibuprofen + Lisinopril
2. **Severity Classification:** Moderate
3. **Pharmacological Mechanism:**
   * **Renal Hemodynamics / Acute Kidney Injury (AKI):** Lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) prevents angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction of the renal *efferent* arteriole, causing efferent vasodilation. Ibuprofen inhibits renal COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes, suppressing vasodilatory renal prostaglandins ($\text{PGE}_2$ and $\text{PGI}_2$) and causing *afferent* renal arteriolar constriction. The combined efferent dilation and afferent constriction significantly drop intraglomerular hydrostatic pressure, decreasing glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and predisposing the patient to AKI.
   * **Antihypertensive Antagonism:** Inhibition of renal prostaglandins by ibuprofen leads to sodium and fluid retention, directly counteracting the blood pressure-lowering effect of lisinopril.
   * **Hyperkalemia:** Both agents impair renal potassium excretion—lisinopril by decreasing aldosterone secretion and ibuprofen by reducing renin release.
4. **Recommended Clinical Action:** Avoid chronic concurrent use of oral NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors. Transition the patient to a non-NSAID strategy for osteoarthritis pain. If short-term ibuprofen use cannot be avoided, monitor baseline and periodic blood pressure, serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and serum potassium levels.

---

### Interaction 3

1. **Interacting Drug Pair:** Warfarin + Lisinopril
2. **Severity Classification:** Minor / No Clinically Significant Interaction
3. **Pharmacological Mechanism:** Lisinopril does not undergo hepatic metabolism via cytochrome P450 enzymes (it is excreted unchanged in the urine) and does not alter hepatic blood flow or plasma protein binding of warfarin. It possesses no intrinsic antiplatelet activity. Thus, there is no significant pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interaction between lisinopril and warfarin.
4. **Recommended Clinical Action:** No dosage adjustments or special interventions are required for this combination. Continue routine INR monitoring as standard for warfarin therapy.

Here is the regulatory analysis under ICH E6(R2) (Integrated Addendum to ICH E6(R1): Guideline for Good Clinical Practice).

---

### Question 1: Centralized-Only Monitoring and Monitor Responsibilities

#### 1. Requirement Statement
Yes, ICH E6(R2) explicitly permits centralized-only monitoring without on-site visits, provided it is justified by a risk assessment. However, for a Phase III oncology trial—which typically involves high protocol complexity, complex dosing, safety reporting (AEs/SAEs), and critical efficacy endpoints—a purely centralized monitoring strategy is difficult to justify without supplementary site oversight or remote source document access. 

Regarding data verification, the guideline mandates that the monitor ensure data reported in Case Report Forms (CRFs) are accurate, complete, and verifiable against source documents. If centralized monitoring is used exclusively, the sponsor must establish automated/remote data processes to evaluate data completeness, consistency, and potential outliers, or ensure remote access to source documentation where legally permissible.

#### 2. Guideline Citations
* **ICH E6(R2) Section 5.18.3 (*Extent and Nature of Monitoring*):** "The sponsor may choose on-site monitoring, a combination of on-site and centralized monitoring, or where justified, centralized monitoring."
* **ICH E6(R2) Section 5.18.3 (*Addendum - Centralized Monitoring*):** Defines centralized monitoring processes as a remote evaluation of accumulating data performed in a timely manner, to identify trends, missing data, protocol deviations, and site errors.
* **ICH E6(R2) Section 5.18.4(g) (*Monitor's Responsibilities - Data Verification*):** Requires the monitor to check "the CRF entries against the source documents and other trial-related records for completeness and accuracy."

#### 3. Exceptions and Conditions
* **Justification Requirement:** Centralized-only monitoring requires a formally documented risk-based monitoring plan (RMP) justifying why on-site visits are not needed for safety or data integrity (Section 5.18.7).
* **Source Data Verification (SDV) Constraints:** Standard centralized monitoring evaluates submitted data rather than raw source records. If source data verification/review (SDV/SDR) is required by the risk plan, the sponsor must ensure remote access to Electronic Health Records (EHR/EMR) in compliance with local privacy regulations (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR).
* **High-Risk Phase III Exception:** Regulatory inspectors (FDA, EMA) generally scrutinize centralized-only monitoring in Phase III oncology trials due to safety risks and primary endpoint verification requirements. On-site or remote SDV visits are usually expected unless alternative remote verification processes are validated.

---

### Question 2: Investigator Responsibilities for Informed Consent

#### 1. Requirement Statement
The investigator (or a designated qualified representative) is responsible for ensuring that freely given written informed consent is obtained from every trial subject (or their legally acceptable representative [LAR]) prior to initiating any trial-related procedures. The investigator must use an IRB/IEC-approved consent form, conduct a thorough discussion without coercion or undue influence, ensure all 20 required elements of informed consent are covered, obtain written signatures and dates, and provide a copy of the signed form to the subject.

#### 2. Guideline Citations
* **ICH E6(R2) Section 4.8.1:** Investigator compliance with GCP and ethical principles derived from the Declaration of Helsinki.
* **ICH E6(R2) Section 4.8.2:** Obligation to obtain written IRB/IEC approval of the written informed consent form and written information before trial initiation.
* **ICH E6(R2) Section 4.8.8:** Written consent form must be signed and personally dated by the subject or the subject's LAR, and by the person who conducted the informed consent discussion, prior to participation.
* **ICH E6(R2) Section 4.8.10:** Detailed listing of mandatory elements to be included in the consent form (e.g., experimental nature, purpose, risks, expected benefits, alternative treatments, confidentiality, right to withdraw).
* **ICH E6(R2) Section 4.8.11:** Investigator must provide a copy of the signed and dated consent form to the subject or LAR.

#### 3. Exceptions and Conditions
* **Emergency Situations / Non-Consentable Subjects (Section 4.8.15):** In emergency trials where prior consent from the subject is impossible and an LAR is not available, enrollment requires specific procedures outlined in the IRB/IEC-approved protocol. Informed consent must be obtained from the subject or LAR as soon as possible thereafter.
* **Inability to Read (Section 4.8.9):** If a subject or LAR is unable to read, an impartial witness must be present during the entire consent discussion. The witness must sign and date the consent form verifying that the information was accurately explained and understood.
* **Minors or Incapacitated Subjects (Section 4.8.12):** Consent must be obtained from the LAR, but the subject should be informed to the extent of their capacity and, if capable, provide assent.

### 1. System Architecture

The system uses a modern full-stack web architecture decoupled into an asynchronous background processing pipeline to handle heavy PDF/Word document extraction and LLM inference without blocking API threads.

#### Components
*   **Client**: Next.js 14 (React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui) hosted on Vercel.
*   **API Gateway / Backend Server**: FastAPI (Python 3.11) hosted on Render (Web Service). Handles Auth validation, document upload presigning, metadata management, and job orchestration.
*   **Task Queue & Worker**: Celery worker running on Render (Background Worker) with Upstash Redis as the message broker. Handles document text extraction, chunking, and calling LLM APIs asynchronously.
*   **Database**: Supabase PostgreSQL database holding users, organizations, contracts, and extracted clause data.
*   **Object Storage**: AWS S3 bucket storing original uploaded files (`.pdf`, `.docx`) and generated export reports.
*   **LLM Provider**: Anthropic API (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) used via the `instructor` Python library for structured JSON output generation.

#### Data Flow
1. User uploads a contract document (`.pdf`/`.docx`) via the Next.js frontend.
2. Frontend requests a pre-signed upload URL from FastAPI backend via `POST /api/v1/contracts/upload-url`.
3. Frontend uploads the raw file directly to AWS S3.
4. On upload completion, Frontend calls `POST /api/v1/contracts` to create a record and trigger the analysis task.
5. FastAPI enqueues a `process_contract` task in Upstash Redis. Celery worker picks up the job.
6. Celery worker downloads the document from S3, parses raw text using PyMuPDF (for PDFs) or `python-docx` (for DOCX), splits text into standard clause blocks, and sends structured prompts to Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
7. Claude 3.5 Sonnet returns extracted clauses, identified risk levels (High, Medium, Low), explanations, and suggested redlines in strict JSON.
8. Celery worker writes the parsed clauses and overall risk summary to Supabase PostgreSQL, then sets contract status to `COMPLETED`.
9. Frontend polls `GET /api/v1/contracts/{id}` (or listens via WebSockets/polling) and renders the split-screen redline review interface.

### 4. Authentication and Authorization Strategy

*   **Provider**: Clerk (or Supabase Auth) managing user sign-ups, SSO, and JWT tokens.
*   **Authentication Token Flow**:
    *   Frontend issues requests with a `Bearer <JWT>` in the `Authorization` HTTP header.
    *   FastAPI backend validates the JWT against Clerk's JWKS endpoint using PyJWT middleware.
*   **Multi-Tenant Isolation**:
    *   Every user token contains custom claims for `user_id` and `organization_id`.
    *   Database query security is enforced at the application layer via FastAPI Dependency Injection (`get_current_tenant_org_id`). All SQL queries automatically include `WHERE organization_id = :tenant_org_id`.
*   **Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)**:
    *   `Admin`: Can invite team members, configure LLM risk sensitivity settings, and delete contracts.
    *   `Member`: Can upload contracts, accept/reject redlines, and export reports.
    *   `Viewer`: Can view contracts and generated redlines in read-only mode.

### 6. AI/LLM Pipeline

#### Document Ingestion & Chunking
1.  **Parsing**: Native PDF parsing using `PyMuPDF` (`fitz`) to preserve page numbers and bounding boxes; `python-docx` for `.docx` files.
2.  **Clause Segmentation**: A dual approach combining rule-based regular expressions (detecting standard headers like `1. Indemnification`, `ARTICLE IV`) and semantic chunking to separate discrete legal provisions into single processing blocks.

#### Structuring LLM Outputs with `instructor` and Pydantic
We enforce strict schema enforcement using Python's `instructor` library wrapped around Claude 3.5 Sonnet (`anthropic`).

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import List, Literal

class ExtractedClause(BaseModel):
    title: str = Field(description="Title or section number of the clause")
    clause_type: str = Field(description="Category: Indemnification, Liability, Termination, Governing Law, Non-Compete, Confidentiality, Other")
    original_text: str = Field(description="Exact verbatim original text extracted from the document")
    risk_level: Literal["LOW", "MEDIUM", "HIGH", "CRITICAL"] = Field(description="Assessed legal risk level")
    risk_explanation: str = Field(description="Clear explanation of why this clause poses a risk to our party")
    suggested_redline: str = Field(description="Revised clause text rewritten to protect our interests")

class ContractAnalysisResult(BaseModel):
    executive_summary: str = Field(description="3-4 sentence overview of the agreement's balance and key risks")
    overall_risk_level: Literal["LOW", "MEDIUM", "HIGH", "CRITICAL"]
    clauses: List[ExtractedClause]
```

#### System Prompting Strategy
*   **System Role**: "You are an elite corporate legal counsel specializing in B2B contract negotiation."
*   **Playbook Context**: Injected context defining risk standard defaults (e.g., "Mutual indemnification is acceptable; unilateral indemnification favoring vendor is HIGH risk. Aggregate liability capped at 12 months' fees is acceptable; unlimited liability is CRITICAL risk.").
*   **Redline Generation**: Using Python `diff-match-patch` on the frontend/backend to generate visual inline additions/deletions diffs based on `original_text` vs `suggested_redline`.

### 11. Top 5 Technical Risks and Specific Mitigations

1.  **Risk: Large Document Context Overhead & High LLM Costs**
    *   *Problem*: Processing a 100-page contract in a single prompt can exceed response output limits, increase latency, and cost over $1.00 per execution.
    *   *Mitigation*: Implement a chunk-and-parse strategy. Chunk documents by major sections or sub-headings first, then pass individual sections through the LLM concurrently using Celery group tasks.
2.  **Risk: Scanned / Non-Searchable Image PDFs**
    *   *Problem*: Standard text extractions (PyMuPDF) return blank text for scanned image-based PDFs.
    *   *Mitigation*: Implement a fallback detection check in the worker: if extracted character count is < 100 on a multi-page document, send pages to AWS Textract or use `pdf2image` + `pytesseract` for OCR processing.
3.  **Risk: LLM JSON Output Formatting Failures**
    *   *Problem*: LLMs returning invalid JSON breaks backend parsing and causes task failures.
    *   *Mitigation*: Enforce `instructor` Pydantic models with automatic retry logic (`max_retries=3`), forcing the model to fix invalid JSON schemas automatically prior to returning to the database.
4.  **Risk: Inconsistent Contract Clause Redline Formatting**
    *   *Problem*: LLM rephrases the entire clause instead of making targeted edits, making diff generation unreadable.
    *   *Mitigation*: Frame system prompts to explicitly demand minimal edits: "Rewrite only the specific sentences containing unacceptable legal risk. Retain as much original text as possible."
5.  **Risk: Processing Timeouts for Async Tasks**
    *   *Problem*: Processing a complex 30-page agreement takes longer than standard HTTP timeout limits (30 seconds).
    *   *Mitigation*: Fully decoupled architecture. S3 upload -> FastAPI returns immediate `201 Accepted` -> Celery worker handles job -> Client UI polls status endpoint every 3 seconds or uses WebSocket events for UI state update.

**Warfarin + ibuprofen — Major**

Mechanism: Dual hit on hemostasis plus GI mucosal injury. Warfarin inhibits vitamin K–dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X). Ibuprofen reversibly inhibits COX-1, reducing platelet thromboxane A2 and impairing aggregation, and depletes gastroprotective prostaglandins, producing erosions/ulcers. The combination therefore impairs both primary and secondary hemostasis on a damaged GI mucosa. Protein-binding displacement is theoretically possible (both highly albumin-bound) but is transient and not the dominant clinical driver. Ibuprofen is not a meaningful CYP2C9 inhibitor, so a large pharmacokinetic rise in S-warfarin is not expected the way it is with some other NSAIDs.

Action: Avoid routine NSAID use in a patient on warfarin. Prefer acetaminophen (or a non-NSAID option) for osteoarthritis. If an NSAID is unavoidable, use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time, add a PPI, counsel on bleeding signs, and increase INR and clinical monitoring. Recheck INR within a few days of starting or stopping regular ibuprofen.

**Ibuprofen + lisinopril — Moderate**

Mechanism: Complementary effects on glomerular hemodynamics and blood-pressure control. ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole (loss of angiotensin II tone), lowering glomerular filtration pressure. NSAIDs inhibit COX-mediated prostaglandin (PGE2/PGI2) production, constricting the afferent arteriole, especially when renal perfusion is already reduced. Together they can drop GFR and precipitate acute kidney injury. Separately, loss of natriuretic prostaglandins causes sodium/water retention and can blunt lisinopril’s antihypertensive effect. Both drugs can also raise potassium (ACEI via reduced aldosterone; NSAID via reduced renin), so hyperkalemia is a secondary risk.

Action: Prefer a non-NSAID analgesic. If ibuprofen is used, keep it PRN and short-term, ensure euvolemia, and monitor blood pressure, serum creatinine/eGFR, and potassium within 1–2 weeks of regular use (sooner in older adults or anyone with CKD, heart failure, or volume depletion). Stop the NSAID if creatinine rises or BP control worsens.

**Warfarin + lisinopril — No well-established clinically significant interaction**

Lisinopril is renally eliminated and is not a CYP2C9/3A4 inhibitor or inducer, so it should not alter S- or R-warfarin clearance. There is no consistent pharmacodynamic effect on coagulation. Isolated older reports of INR changes with some ACE inhibitors exist, but they are not a reliable class effect and do not support a standard interaction rating for this pair. No change in warfarin dose or extra INR checks is required solely because lisinopril is co-prescribed.

**Overall clinical note:** The highest-priority problem on this list is warfarin + ibuprofen (bleeding, especially GI). The next is ibuprofen + lisinopril (AKI and loss of BP control). Using all three together is particularly unfavorable in older adults: NSAID-related GI injury plus anticoagulation, plus NSAID/ACEI renal risk. Acetaminophen (or topical NSAID if appropriate) is the cleaner analgesic choice here.

**Yes — ICH E6(R2) permits centralized-only monitoring where justified, but it is not the default and must be documented. Informed consent remains an investigator (not monitor) obligation under Section 4.8.**

Note: ICH E6(R3) was adopted in January 2025 and is now the current ICH GCP text in implementing regions. The answers below address **E6(R2)** as requested. Section numbers should be verified against the official ICH E6(R2) PDF if used in a submission or SOP.

## 1. Centralized-only monitoring and the monitor’s data-verification duties

### Requirement

ICH E6(R2) **does permit** a sponsor to use centralized monitoring only, **with no on-site visits**, but only **where that strategy is justified** and the rationale is documented (typically in the monitoring plan). The baseline expectation in the original 5.18.3 text remains that **on-site monitoring is generally needed**; centralized-only monitoring is a justified exception, not the starting assumption.

The R2 Addendum explicitly expanded flexibility:

> The sponsor may choose on-site monitoring, a combination of on-site and centralized monitoring, or, **where justified, centralized monitoring**. The sponsor should document the rationale for the chosen monitoring strategy (e.g., in the monitoring plan).

Centralized monitoring is defined as remote evaluation of accumulating data, performed in a timely manner by appropriately qualified staff (e.g., data managers, biostatisticians). It can complement or **reduce the extent and/or frequency** of on-site monitoring and is intended to help distinguish reliable from potentially unreliable data.

### Citation

- **ICH E6(R2) 5.18.1** — Purpose of monitoring (subject protection; data accurate, complete, and **verifiable from source documents**; protocol/GCP/regulatory compliance).
- **ICH E6(R2) 5.18.3** — Extent and nature of monitoring; “in general there is a need for on-site monitoring… however, in exceptional circumstances” central monitoring plus training, meetings, and extensive written guidance may suffice; statistically controlled sampling may be used for data verification.
- **ICH E6(R2) 5.18.3 Addendum** — Risk-based, prioritized monitoring; on-site, mixed, or **justified centralized-only**; document the rationale.
- **ICH E6(R2) 5.18.4** — Monitor’s responsibilities (performed “when relevant and necessary to the trial and the trial site”).
- **ICH E6(R2) 5.18.4(k)** — Verify that source documents and other trial records are accurate, complete, kept up to date, and maintained.
- **ICH E6(R2) 5.18.4(m)** — Check accuracy and completeness of CRF entries, source documents, and other trial-related records **against each other**, including:
  - protocol-required data reported accurately on CRFs and **consistent with source documents**;
  - dose/therapy modifications documented;
  - AEs, concomitant medications, and intercurrent illnesses reported per protocol;
  - missed visits/tests/examinations clearly reported;
  - withdrawals/dropouts reported and explained.
- **ICH E6(R2) 5.18.4(e)** — Verify that written informed consent was obtained before each subject’s participation.
- **ICH E6(R2) 5.18.6** — Monitoring reports.
- **ICH E6(R2) 5.18.7 Addendum** — Monitoring plan: tailored to subject-protection and data-integrity risks; describe strategy, responsibilities, methods, and rationale; emphasize critical data and processes.

Related sponsor QC/QA: **5.1.1–5.1.3** (quality assurance/control; data handled to allow reporting, interpretation, and verification; agreements with investigators/institutions and CROs).

### Exceptions / conditions (material for this Phase III oncology plan)

1. **Justification is mandatory.** “Where justified” (5.18.3 Addendum) and “exceptional circumstances” (5.18.3 body) both apply. A one-line statement that the trial will be “centrally monitored only” is not enough. The monitoring plan must explain **why** on-site visits are unnecessary for *this* protocol’s risks.
2. **Risk-based, not convenience-based.** 5.18.3 Addendum and 5.18.7 require a systematic, prioritized, risk-based approach focused on critical data and processes. Phase III oncology typically involves high medical risk, investigational product accountability, serious/unexpected AEs, complex eligibility, survival or tumor-response endpoints, and frequent protocol complexity. Those factors cut **against** a no-visit model unless residual risk is demonstrably controlled by other means (e.g., validated EHR/EDC source access, real-time safety signal detection, IP chain-of-custody systems, targeted for-cause visit triggers).
3. **Source-data verification still applies.** 5.18.1(b) and 5.18.4(k)/(m) are not waived because monitoring is remote. If the monitor never sees source documents, the sponsor must show another reliable method to confirm CRF–source consistency (remote source access, certified copies, direct EHR feeds, etc.). Absence of a verification method is a GCP gap, not a permitted efficiency.
4. **On-site activities in 5.18.4 remain “when relevant and necessary.”** Facilities, investigational product storage, consent process observation, delegation, and eligibility are listed as monitor duties. A centralized-only plan must state how each relevant duty is discharged remotely or why it is not necessary — and when a **for-cause on-site visit** will be triggered (the Addendum lists site selection for targeted on-site monitoring as a use of centralized review).
5. **Document the strategy before the trial starts.** 5.18.7: plan, methods, parties, rationale, critical data/processes, and applicable SOPs. Changes should be controlled.
6. **Regional inspectors may still expect some on-site presence** for a Phase III oncology RCT even though ICH text allows a justified centralized-only model. ICH sets a floor, not a shield against FDA/EMA/PMDA inspection findings if the justification is weak.

**Practical regulatory position for this scenario:** ICH E6(R2) does **not** forbid centralized-only monitoring. For a Phase III randomized oncology trial, a no-visit plan is legally available only if the sponsor can defend it as risk-proportionate and still meet 5.18.1 purposes, including source verification. A hybrid model (centralized review plus targeted/for-cause on-site visits) is the reading most consistent with both 5.18.3 (“in general… on-site”) and the R2 Addendum.

## 2. Investigator responsibilities for informed consent (ICH E6(R2))

### Requirement

Informed consent is an **investigator responsibility**. The investigator must obtain and document consent in compliance with applicable law, GCP, and the ethical principles originating in the Declaration of Helsinki; use only IRB/IEC-approved consent materials; avoid coercion; give adequate information and time; obtain a signed and personally dated consent **before** any trial-specific procedures; and keep the subject informed if new information arises.

The monitor verifies that consent was obtained (5.18.4(e)); the monitor does **not** obtain consent.

### Citation and operative rules

**ICH E6(R2) 4.8** is the governing section. Key obligations:

| Topic | Section | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Legal/ethical basis; IRB/IEC approval of ICF and written information **before** the trial | **4.8.1** | Investigator complies with applicable regulatory requirements, GCP, and Declaration of Helsinki principles. Written IRB/IEC approval of the ICF and any other written subject information is required before the trial begins. |
| Updates when new information arises | **4.8.2** | Revise ICF/written information when important new information may affect willingness to participate; obtain IRB/IEC approval **before use**; inform the subject or legally acceptable representative (LAR) in a timely manner; **document** that communication. |
| No coercion or undue influence | **4.8.3** | Neither the investigator nor trial staff may coerce or unduly influence a subject to enroll or continue. |
| No waiver of legal rights / no release from negligence | **4.8.4** | Oral and written information, including the ICF, must not waive or appear to waive legal rights, or release the investigator, institution, sponsor, or agents from liability for negligence. |
| Who informs the subject | **4.8.5** | The investigator, **or a person designated by the investigator**, fully informs the subject or, if the subject cannot consent, the LAR, of all pertinent aspects, including the written information and the IRB/IEC opinion. |
| Understandable language | **4.8.6** | Oral and written information, including the ICF, should be as non-technical as practical and understandable to the subject, LAR, and impartial witness where applicable. |
| Time, questions, voluntary decision | **4.8.7** | Before consent is obtained, provide ample time and opportunity to inquire and decide. Answer all questions to the subject’s or LAR’s satisfaction. |
| Signature and dating **before** participation | **4.8.8** | Prior to participation, the written ICF is signed and **personally dated** by the subject or LAR **and** by the person who conducted the consent discussion. |
| Illiterate subject or LAR — impartial witness | **4.8.9** | If the subject or LAR cannot read, an impartial witness must be present for the entire discussion; witness signs and dates, attesting that information was accurately explained and apparently understood and that consent was freely given. |
| Required content of discussion and ICF | **4.8.10(a)–(t)** | Trial involves research; purpose; treatments and probability of assignment; procedures including invasive ones; subject’s responsibilities; experimental aspects; reasonably foreseeable risks/inconveniences; reasonably expected benefits (or no intended clinical benefit); alternatives; compensation/treatment for injury; prorated payment; anticipated expenses; voluntary participation and freedom to refuse/withdraw without penalty or loss of benefits; monitors/auditors/IRB/IEC/regulators may access medical records without violating confidentiality and that by signing the ICF the subject/LAR authorizes that access; records will be confidential to the extent permitted by applicable laws; if results are published identity will remain confidential; subject/LAR will be informed in a timely manner if information becomes available that may be relevant to willingness to continue; foreseeable circumstances/reasons for termination of participation; expected duration; approximate number of subjects. |
| Copies | **4.8.11** | Before participation, provide a copy of the signed and dated ICF and any other written information. During the trial, provide copies of signed/dated updated ICFs and amendments to written information. |
| Subjects who can be enrolled only via LAR (e.g., minors, severe dementia) | **4.8.12** | Inform the subject to the extent compatible with understanding; if capable, the subject should also sign and personally date the ICF. |
| Non-therapeutic trials | **4.8.13–4.8.14** | Generally only in subjects who personally consent (**4.8.13**), except LAR consent is allowed if all of **4.8.14(a)–(e)** are met: objectives cannot be met in consenting subjects; foreseeable risks low; negative impact minimized and low; not prohibited by law; IRB/IEC expressly approves inclusion of such subjects. Unless an exception is justified, conduct in patients with the disease/condition of interest; monitor closely; withdraw if unduly distressed. |
| Emergency situations (prior consent not possible) | **4.8.15** | Seek LAR consent if the LAR is present. If neither subject nor LAR can consent, enrollment may proceed only under protocol-described measures with documented IRB/IEC approval, protecting rights, safety, and well-being and complying with law. Inform the subject or LAR as soon as possible and request consent to continue (and other consent as appropriate per 4.8.10). |

Related investigator sections (not a substitute for 4.8):

- **4.1.1** — Investigator qualified by education, training, and experience.
- **4.3.2** — Medical decisions/care by a qualified physician (or dentist, as applicable).
- **4.5.1** — Conduct the trial in compliance with the protocol agreed with the sponsor and given IRB/IEC approval (consent process is protocol-specified).
- **4.9.1–4.9.3** — Accurate records; corrections; essential documents available for monitor/auditor/IRB/IEC/regulator.

Sponsor/monitor interface (not investigator consent duties, but relevant to the CRO monitoring plan):

- **5.18.4(e)** — Monitor verifies written informed consent was obtained **before** each subject’s participation.
- **8.2.3 / 8.3.12** (essential documents) — blank ICF and signed ICFs are essential documents.

### Exceptions / conditions

1. **Delegation is allowed; accountability is not.** 4.8.5 permits a designated person to conduct the discussion, but the investigator remains responsible for the process and for ensuring the designee is qualified and listed on the delegation log.
2. **IRB/IEC approval is a precondition**, including for every revised ICF (4.8.1, 4.8.2). Using an unapproved version is a consent violation.
3. **Timing is absolute for standard enrollment:** signature and personal dates **before** any trial-specific procedure (4.8.8, 4.8.11). Screening procedures that are not standard care require prior consent.
4. **LAR and witness pathways** (4.8.9, 4.8.12–4.8.15) are the only ICH-recognized alternatives to personal subject consent. Local law on who may serve as LAR controls; ICH does not override it (4.8.1).
5. **Emergency waiver** (4.8.15) applies only when prior consent is not possible **and** the protocol plus IRB/IEC have pre-specified protective measures. It is uncommon as a routine pathway in a planned Phase III oncology RCT, but it can arise (e.g., certain acute presentations). It is not a general exemption.
6. **Re-consent** is required when important new information may affect willingness to continue (4.8.2) — protocol amendments, new safety findings, and material ICF changes.
7. **Oncology-specific practical points** (conditions, not extra ICH sections): capacity may fluctuate; caregivers are not automatically LARs; language/health-literacy of 4.8.6 is frequently an inspection finding; and centralized monitoring does **not** reduce the investigator’s 4.8 duties. If the CRO will not be on site, the monitoring plan still needs a method to confirm 4.8.8 timing and completeness (remote review of signed ICFs, certified copies, or equivalent).

---

**Bottom line for the CRO plan:** E6(R2) 5.18.3 Addendum allows centralized-only monitoring if justified and documented; 5.18.1 and 5.18.4 still require a credible way to protect subjects and verify source data, including that consent was obtained before participation. Investigator consent duties sit entirely in **4.8** and are unchanged by the monitoring model. For a Phase III oncology RCT, treat centralized-only as a high-justification exception and build explicit for-cause on-site triggers, or expect inspectors to challenge the plan against 5.18.3’s “in general… on-site” language.

# ContractLens MVP — 7-Day Build Plan

**Product:** B2B SaaS AI contract review assistant  
**Team:** 3 engineers (A: backend/platform, B: AI/worker, C: frontend)  
**Constraint:** ship a demoable, multi-tenant MVP in 7 days that can take real PDF/DOCX uploads, extract clauses, flag risks, suggest redlines, and emit a summary report.

**Locked stack**

| Layer | Choice |
|---|---|
| Frontend | Next.js 15 (App Router), TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, TanStack Query v5, Zustand |
| Backend API | FastAPI, Python 3.12, Pydantic v2, SQLAlchemy 2.0, Alembic |
| Worker | same Python repo, `arq` + Redis |
| Auth | Clerk (Organizations + JWT session tokens) |
| DB | Neon Postgres 16 |
| Files | Cloudflare R2 (S3 API) via `boto3` |
| Queue/cache | Upstash Redis |
| AI | Anthropic Claude: Haiku for segmentation, Sonnet for risk + redlines + report |
| Extraction | PyMuPDF (`fitz`) for PDF, `python-docx` for Word |
| Hosting | Vercel (web), Railway (API + worker) |
| Email (transactional, optional) | Resend — only “analysis complete” |
| Observability | Sentry (FE + BE), structured JSON logs, Railway logs |
| PDF report | WeasyPrint (HTML → PDF) |

No Kubernetes, no microservices, no Terraform. One monorepo: `/apps/web`, `/apps/api`.

---

## 1. System architecture

**Components**

1. **Web (Vercel)** — Next.js app. Auth via Clerk. Uploads go **directly to R2** with a presigned PUT. The browser never streams multi-MB files through FastAPI.
2. **API (Railway)** — FastAPI. Authn via Clerk JWT. CRUD for contracts, clauses, risks, redlines, reports. Enqueues analysis jobs. Serves report download.
3. **Worker (Railway, second process)** — `arq` consumer. Pulls `analyze_contract` jobs. Downloads file from R2, extracts text, runs the LLM pipeline, writes rows, marks job terminal.
4. **Postgres (Neon)** — source of truth. Every business row has `org_id`.
5. **R2** — raw uploads + generated report PDFs. Keys: `org/{org_id}/contracts/{contract_id}/source.{ext}` and `.../report.pdf`.
6. **Redis (Upstash)** — job queue + short-lived job progress keys (`job:{id}:pct`).
7. **Anthropic** — LLM calls from the worker only. API key never leaves Railway.
8. **Sentry** — exceptions from Next.js, FastAPI, and worker.

**Data flow (happy path)**

1. User signs in (Clerk). Frontend reads `org_id` from active Clerk Organization.
2. `POST /v1/contracts` creates a `contracts` row (`status=pending_upload`) and returns an R2 presigned PUT + `contract_id`.
3. Browser PUTs the file to R2. Frontend calls `POST /v1/contracts/{id}/finalize` with `byte_size`, `content_type`, `sha256`.
4. API sets `status=queued`, inserts `analysis_jobs`, enqueues `analyze_contract(job_id)` on Redis.
5. Worker: download → extract text/pages → persist `contract_texts` → run LLM pipeline → write `clauses`, `risks`, `redlines`, `reports` → upload report PDF to R2 → `status=ready` (or `failed`).
6. Frontend polls `GET /v1/contracts/{id}` (and `/jobs/{id}`) every 2s until terminal, then loads clauses/risks/redlines/report.
7. User edits a suggested redline (accept / reject / edit). PATCH persists reviewer decision. Regenerating the report is a separate explicit action.

**Sync vs async:** all LLM work is async. API requests are CRUD + enqueue only. Hard timeout on API: 15s. Worker job timeout: 12 minutes.

**Tenant isolation:** `org_id` taken from the verified JWT, never from the client body. Every query is `WHERE org_id = :jwt_org`. R2 keys are prefixed by `org_id`. Presigned URLs are scoped to that key.

## 3. Backend API

Base: `https://api.<your-domain>/v1`  
Auth header: `Authorization: Bearer <clerk_session_jwt>`  
All JSON. Org is **only** from the JWT (`org_id` claim after membership resolve).  
Idempotency: `Idempotency-Key` required on `POST /contracts` and `POST /contracts/{id}/analyze`.

**Health**

`GET /health` → `{ "ok": true, "version": "0.1.0" }`  
`GET /ready` → checks Postgres + Redis; 503 if down.

**Contracts**

`POST /v1/contracts`

Request:
```json
{
  "title": "MSA - Acme Corp",
  "counterparty": "Acme Corp",
  "filename": "acme-msa.pdf",
  "content_type": "application/pdf",
  "byte_size": 482113
}
```

Response `201`:
```json
{
  "id": "c_01J...",
  "status": "pending_upload",
  "upload": {
    "url": "https://r2-presigned...",
    "method": "PUT",
    "headers": { "Content-Type": "application/pdf" },
    "expires_in_sec": 900
  }
}
```

`POST /v1/contracts/{id}/finalize`

Request: `{ "sha256": "b5c3..." }`  
Response `202`: `{ "id": "c_01J...", "status": "queued", "job_id": "j_01J..." }`

`GET /v1/contracts?status=ready&q=acme&limit=20&cursor=...`

Response:
```json
{
  "items": [
    {
      "id": "c_01J...",
      "title": "MSA - Acme Corp",
      "counterparty": "Acme Corp",
      "status": "ready",

```

`POST /v1/contracts/{id}/analyze` — re-run. `202` + new `job_id`. Allowed from `ready` or `failed`.

**Jobs**

`GET /v1/jobs/{id}`

```json
{
  "id": "j_01J...",
  "contract_id": "c_01J...",
```

## 4. Authentication and authorization

**Authn**

- Clerk handles signup, login, invites, org creation, session refresh.
- Next.js uses `@clerk/nextjs`. Middleware protects all routes except `/sign-in`, `/sign-up`.
- FastAPI dependency `get_principal()`:
  1. Read Bearer token.
  2. Verify JWT against Clerk JWKS (cache 10 min).
  3. Require `org_id` in session claims.
  4. Upsert `users` + `organizations` + `memberships` on first seen (`clerk_user_id` / `clerk_org_id`).
  5. Return `Principal(user_id, org_id, role, clerk_user_id)`.

No custom passwords. No API keys in MVP (out of scope).

**Authz (RBAC)**

| Action | owner | admin | reviewer | viewer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Upload / re-analyze | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Accept/edit redlines | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Download report | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Delete contract | ✓ | ✓ | | |
| Invite members (Clerk) | ✓ | ✓ | | |
| Change roles | ✓ | ✓ | | |

Enforced in a `require_role(*roles)` dependency. Viewers can open the review UI read-only.

**Tenant rules**

- Every SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE includes `org_id = principal.org_id`.
- Presigned R2 keys always start with `org/{org_id}/`.
- Cross-org IDOR tests are in the day-5 checklist (guess UUID from another org → 404, not 403).

**Webhook:** Clerk `user.created` / `organizationMembership.created` hit `POST /v1/internal/clerk` (svix signature) to keep memberships in sync if someone is removed mid-session.

## 6. AI / LLM pipeline

Worker stages. Each stage updates `analysis_jobs.stage` + `progress_pct`. All LLM calls use **JSON schema / tool use** (Anthropic structured outputs). Temperature 0. Retry once on parse failure with a repair prompt. Persist raw model output in logs, not in Postgres (too large); persist token usage on the job.

**Stage 0 — Ingest (0–10%)**  
Download from R2.  
PDF: PyMuPDF, page-by-page text, keep page breaks. Reject if extracted text < 400 chars (likely scan) with `error_code=SCANNED_OR_EMPTY`.  
DOCX: `python-docx` paragraphs; synthetic page breaks every ~3k chars for location hints.  
Write `contract_texts`.

**Stage 1 — Segment clauses (10–40%) — Haiku**  
Split `full_text` into overlapping windows of ~6k tokens, 400-token overlap, prefer split on headings (`Article`, `Section`, numbered clauses).  
Per window, tool schema:

```json
{
  "clauses": [
    {
      "heading": "string",
      "clause_type": "indemnity|limitation_of_liability|...|other",
      "text": "verbatim excerpt",
      "page_start": 1,
      "page_end": 1
    }
  ]
}
```

Merge windows: exact-text dedupe, then fuzzy (rapidfuzz `token_set_ratio > 92`) to drop overlap dupes. Assign `ordinal`, map `char_start/char_end` via first occurrence in `full_text`.

**Stage 2 — Risk classify (40–65%) — Sonnet**  
Input: system playbook `rules_json` (≈15 rules) + batches of 8 clauses.  
Schema:

```json
{
  "risks": [
    {
      "clause_ordinal": 4,
      "playbook_rule_id": "liability_uncapped",
      "severity": "critical",
      "title": "Uncapped indemnity",
      "rationale": "...",
      "recommendation": "...",
      "confidence": 0.86
    }
  ]
}
```

If no rule fires, emit nothing. Do not invent rules. Prompt forbids flagging missing boilerplate that is merely “not buyer-friendly” unless a playbook rule matches.

**Default playbook (seed) — 15 rules, examples:**  
uncapped indemnity · missing liability cap · cap excludes fees-paid standard · auto-renewal without notice window · unilateral termination for convenience (vendor-only) · IP assignment of pre-existing materials · missing DPA / SCCs when personal data present · governing law not in allowlist · unlimited audit rights · broad non-solicit · payment net-90+ · missing insurance minimums · perpetual confidentiality with no residual knowledge · assignment without consent · warranty disclaimer of merchantability **and** fitness with no performance warranty left.

**Stage 3 — Redlines (65–85%) — Sonnet**  
Only clauses with `critical|high|medium` risks. One call per clause (keeps edits local).  
Schema: `{ original_text, suggested_text, explanation }`.  
Constraints in prompt: preserve defined terms; do not delete the whole clause; prefer inserting a cap / carve-out / notice period; mark `[COUNTERPARTY]` / `[CLIENT]` placeholders only if a name is unknown.

**Stage 4 — Report (85–95%) — Sonnet**  
Inputs: title, counterparty, risk histogram, top 10 risks, accepted-or-proposed redline count.  
Output markdown: Executive summary (6–10 lines) · Deal-breakers · Negotiation priorities · Residual low risks.  
Then WeasyPrint HTML template → PDF → R2. Write `reports`.

**Stage 5 — Persist (95–100%)**  
Single transaction: insert clauses/risks/redlines/report, set contract `ready`, job `succeeded`. On any unhandled exception: rollback that transaction, job `failed`, contract `failed`, `error_code` set. Extracted text is kept so retry skips Stage 0.

**Model routing**

| Step | Model | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Segment | `claude-haiku-4-5` (or current Haiku) | cheap, high volume |
| Classify / redline / report | `claude-sonnet-4-5` (or current Sonnet) | legal nuance |

**Prompt versioning:** `prompts/*.md` + `PROMPT_VERSION=2026-08-13.1` stored on `analysis_jobs.model_usage_json`. Changing a prompt does not silently mix with old outputs.

**Determinism aids:** temperature 0, fixed playbook, clause text verbatim, schema validation via Pydantic before insert.

## 8. Observability, logging, error handling

**Logs**  
JSON to stdout: `ts, level, request_id, org_id, user_id, contract_id, job_id, event, duration_ms`.  
`request_id` = `X-Request-Id` or generated ULID. Propagated API → worker via job payload.

**Metrics (minimum, no Datadog in MVP)**  
Log-based: job duration by stage, LLM tokens, extract page count, status transitions. Railway CPU/RAM alerts at 80%.

**Sentry**  
- FastAPI: `sentry-sdk[fastapi]`, ignore `HTTPException` 4xx.  
- Worker: capture exceptions with job/contract tags.  
- Next.js: `@sentry/nextjs` on API proxy failures and review-page crashes.  
Alert: any `error` in worker, or job fail rate > 20% in 15 min (manual check day 1–7; simple Sentry alert after).

**Error handling**

| Class | Behavior |
|---|---|
| Validation / 4xx | Pydantic → `VALIDATION_ERROR`, no Sentry |
| Unsupported / empty PDF | `failed` + user-visible reason, no retry loop |
| Anthropic 429 / 5xx | worker retries 3x, exp backoff 5/20/60s, then fail job |
| JSON parse fail | 1 repair call; then fail stage |
| API DB outage | 503 `ready` check; frontend toast |
| Upload > 25 MB | rejected before presign |
| Worker crash mid-job | `arq` retry once; `attempt` incremented; third failure is terminal |

**Frontend:** React error boundary around review workspace. Job `failed` shows `error_message` + Retry. Never show stack traces.

**Audit:** `audit_events` on upload, analyze, redline decision, report download. Enough for a first security questionnaire, not SOC2.

**Usage assumptions (state these in the pricing memo)**  
- 20 orgs, 100 MAU.  
- 8 analyses / user / month → **800 jobs**.  
- Avg contract: 15 pages, ~12k tokens extracted text.  
- Per job tokens (after routing): Haiku 25k in / 6k out; Sonnet 20k in / 8k out.  
- Storage: 800 × 2 MB source + 0.4 MB PDF ≈ 2 GB, retained 90 days.  
- API traffic: negligible next to LLM.

## 11. Top 5 technical risks and mitigations

**1. Garbage extraction (scans, image-only PDFs, weird Word)**  
Mitigation: reject low-text PDFs with a clear error (`SCANNED_OR_EMPTY`). Support digital PDF + DOCX only. Fixture tests on 10 real files day 3. OCR explicitly out of MVP. Show page_count and a text preview so users see what the model saw.

**2. LLM schema drift / hallucinated clauses**  
Mitigation: structured outputs + Pydantic; drop clauses that are not substrings of `full_text` (allow whitespace normalize); one repair retry; golden-set CI that fails the build if “uncapped indemnity” is missed on the fixture MSA or if extra clauses aren’t in source. Temperature 0. Prompt: “verbatim excerpts only.”

**3. 7-day schedule slip / AI rabbit hole**  
Mitigation: Day 2 must work without LLM. Day 7 demo uses 3 precomputed contracts. Playbook is hardcoded JSON. No custom model training, no Word add-in, no compare-two-contracts. If Day 4 redlines are late, ship classify + summary first; redlines can be “recommendation text” without full rewrite.

**4. Multi-tenant IDOR / presigned URL leak**  
Mitigation: `org_id` only from JWT; integration test suite that creates two orgs and asserts 404; R2 keys prefixed; presign TTL 15 min; no listing permission on the bucket; viewer role cannot upload. Do this on Day 6 before any external demo.

**5. Latency and Anthropic rate limits during a live demo**  
Mitigation: async jobs + progress UI; pre-warmed demo data; worker timeout 12 min; exponential backoff; `arq` max 2 concurrent LLM jobs to stay under TPM; if Sonnet is slow, classify in batches of 8 not 1. Never call Anthropic from the request thread.

## 12. Explicitly out of MVP scope

- Scanned PDF / OCR / handwriting.
- `.doc` (legacy), RTF, images, email `.msg`, zip batches.
- Microsoft Word add-in, Google Docs, track-changes `.docx` export (report PDF only).
- Contract-to-contract compare, playbook editor, customer-specific clause libraries.
- Negotiation chat / “ask the contract” Q&A.
- E-signature, clause negotiation workflows, comments @mentions.
- SSO/SAML, SCIM, custom API keys, public REST for customers, webhooks out.
- On-prem, VPC deploy, customer-managed keys, data residency picker.
- SOC 2 / ISO evidence beyond the thin `audit_events` table.
- Billing integration (Stripe), self-serve plan upgrades.
- Mobile apps, responsive polish below desktop.
- Human-in-the-loop review marketplace, lawyer network.
- Fine-tuned models, RAG over the customer’s prior contracts (no vector DB).
- Real-time collaboration (presence, CRDT).
- Versioning of the source file / redline history beyond current decision state.
- Auto-detect governing-law allowlists per org (hardcode US/DE/UK in playbook text only).
- Multi-language contracts (English only).
- SLA, uptime credits, dedicated support.

**MVP definition of done:** one org’s legal team can upload an English digital PDF or DOCX, get clauses + severity-tagged risks + suggested redlines, accept/edit them, and download a summary PDF, with Clerk-based team roles and org isolation, in production, in 7 days.
