**Total estimated monthly run rate: about $600 to $700**, or about $6 to $7 per active user per month. Cost per analyzed contract is about $1.50 to $1.75 all-in, with AI at about $0.35 to $0.40 per contract. The largest levers are RDS and Fargate, both of which can be right-sized after the pilot. Estimates exclude engineering labor and any enterprise support plan.

---

## 11. Top 5 Technical Risks and Mitigations

**Risk 1: LLM misses clauses or misclassifies them (false negatives on critical risks).**
- Mitigation: Use the heuristic section boundaries as hints so segmentation is anchored to the document's own structure. Require the must-have checklist to run independently of the LLM output: if a must-have clause type is not found by the classifier, surface it as "missing or unidentified" for human review rather than silently passing it. Run the 40-contract eval harness before each release with regression thresholds (for example, clause F1 at or above 0.85 and critical-risk recall at or above 0.90 on the labeled set). Keep the reviewer in the loop with clear "this was AI-generated" labeling and confidence scores.

**Risk 2: Hallucinated evidence or redlines (quotes not in the contract, or redlines that change more than intended).**
- Mitigation: Enforce verbatim `evidence_quote` and `original_text` checks in code. Reject any output that fails the substring check, then retry once and drop if it still fails. Redlines replace only the exact matched span, never full clauses. A second-pass verifier model checks rationale against the quote. Findings failing grounding are hidden from default views and logged for review. Redlines are never auto-applied; the user must explicitly accept.

**Risk 3: Confidentiality and data privacy concerns from legal customers (contracts contain sensitive data).**
- Mitigation: Confirm with the LLM provider that the API terms prohibit training on customer data and set zero data retention where available. Encrypt at rest (KMS) and in transit (TLS). Store per-tenant data with RLS and separate S3 prefixes per org. Never log contract text. Provide a data retention setting and a hard-delete path that purges S3 objects, database rows, and embeddings within 30 days. Put a DPA and sub-processor list in front of pilot customers before they upload real contracts. Keep a clear documented list of what is sent to the LLM.

**Risk 4: Parsing quality and scanned or messy documents (broken tables, headers and footers, OCR errors).**
- Mitigation: Strip repeated headers and footers by detecting text repeated across pages. Preserve numbering by normalizing list markers before segmentation. Route scanned PDFs to Textract with a visible "OCR mode" indicator and a lower default confidence. Set a minimum parse quality check (text density per page, character error heuristics) and fail with a clear message ("This document could not be read reliably. Please upload a text-based PDF or DOCX.") rather than producing bad output. Track parse failure rates by source type and iterate after the pilot.

**Risk 5: Latency, cost overruns, and scope creep in a 7-day build.**
- Mitigation: Process long contracts in parallel chunks with a per-job cost ceiling (for example, a maximum of 300k tokens per job, with the reviewer notified if exceeded). Use prompt caching for the playbook and system prompts, and route verifier and summary tasks to cheaper models. Set per-org rate limits and a daily spend alarm. For schedule risk, lock scope on Day 1 using the out-of-scope list in Section 12, hold a daily 15-minute standup, and designate a cut list in advance (for example, PDF report styling, SSE and fallback to polling, and the second playbook type) that can be dropped without breaking the core flow.

---

## 12. Explicitly Out of MVP Scope

- Native Microsoft Word tracked-changes export (redlines are shown in the UI and included as text in the PDF report only).
- Real-time collaborative editing, comments threads between multiple reviewers, and @mentions.
- Negotiation workflows, counterparty portal, or sending redlines to counterparties via email.
- E-signature integration (DocuSign, Adobe Sign) and contract lifecycle management features (repository search across all contracts, obligation tracking, renewal reminders).
- Integrations with CLM or CRM systems (Salesforce, Ironclad, Icertis, SharePoint, Google Drive, Box).
- Non-English contracts and multilingual clause classification.
- Fine-tuned or custom-trained models. The MVP uses hosted foundation models with prompts and playbooks.
- Automated legal advice or guaranteed compliance determinations. The product is positioned as an assistant that requires attorney review.
- Multi-region deployment, SOC 2 Type II or ISO 27001 certification (the MVP follows security practices and begins the SOC 2 readiness process after the pilot).
- SSO via SAML or SCIM provisioning (Clerk Google login and magic link only for MVP; enterprise SSO is a post-pilot item).
- Self-serve billing, usage metering dashboards, and invoicing (billing is handled manually during the pilot).
- Mobile apps and native clients.
- Full-text search across extracted clauses and advanced analytics (portfolio risk trends, benchmarking against market data).
- Bulk upload of hundreds of contracts at once (MVP supports one document per upload, with multiple uploads allowed sequentially).
- Custom OCR tuning for handwritten or heavily annotated documents.
- Version comparison between contract drafts (a single document version is analyzed per job).

## Quick read of your problem

Slack overload and duplicate work are usually the same disease with two symptoms: there's no single place that says *what work exists, who owns it, and whether it's already been claimed*. So every request gets broadcast to everyone (noise), and two people pick up the same thing because neither can see the other (duplication).

## Suggested solution

Build a thin **triage layer** between Slack and wherever work actually lives. Not a new tool — a routing and dedupe skin over what you already have.

1. **Intake funnel** — Work enters through one path (a slash command like `/task`, or a ✅ reaction on a message) instead of DMs and free-text channel posts.
2. **Dedupe check** — On creation, the bot fuzzy-matches against open items by title, requester, and any pasted links, then asks "looks like this might be #412 — join it or create new?"
3. **Owner + status** — Every item gets exactly one owner and a status. No owner, no work.
4. **Digest instead of pings** — Kill per-message notifications. Two or three scheduled digests a day, with @mention reserved for genuine blockers only.
5. **Channel hygiene** — Default to threads, mute bot/CI channels, auto-archive anything stale.

If you have no engineers to build it, the buy-side equivalent is a shared-inbox or issue tracker with a Slack integration (Linear, Height, Notion, Front) plus strict intake rules. The tool matters less than the rule that *Slack is for talking, the board is for work*.

## Assumptions I'm making (correct me)

- You're on Slack and can install apps / write a bot.
- The duplicate work is human coordination, not two systems literally syncing the same data.
- You have *some* existing tracker, even if it's a messy Notion page.
- You have authority or a manager who can enforce a process change.

## Clarifying questions

1. How big is the team, and what's the mix (engineers, ops, support, mixed)?
2. Roughly how many Slack messages and channels per day are we talking — 200 or 20,000?
3. What does "duplicate work" look like concretely: two people assigned the same task, two people independently solving the same problem, or the same question answered over and over?
4. Where does work live today — Jira, Linear, Notion, Asana, GitHub Issues, or literally nowhere?
5. What's generating the notification volume — humans, CI/CD bots, monitoring alerts, external tools?
6. Can you build, or do you need something off-the-shelf? Any budget?
7. Any hard constraints: Enterprise Grid, compliance, on-prem, IT approval process?
8. Who owns this problem — is there one person who can say "this is how we do it now" and have it stick?
9. What would success look like in 30 days? (Fewer pings? Zero duplicate tickets? Faster response time?)

# Regulatory Assessment: Centralized-Only Monitoring and Informed Consent Under ICH E6(R2)

**Scope note:** ICH E6(R2) (adopted 2016) was superseded by ICH E6(R3) (Step 4, May 2023). The analysis below is anchored to R2 as requested, with a brief R3 cross-reference at the end.

---

## Question 1: Does ICH E6(R2) permit centralized-only monitoring with no on-site visits?

### Requirement

**Yes — but only "where justified," and the justification must be documented.** R2 explicitly introduced centralized monitoring as a permissible standalone strategy. However, the older language in the same section still states that on-site monitoring is generally expected, creating a tension that the sponsor must resolve through a risk-based rationale.

### Citation

- **ICH E6(R2) Section 5.18.3** — the operative provision: *"The sponsor should develop a systematic, prioritized, risk-based approach to monitoring clinical trials. … The sponsor may choose on-site monitoring, a combination of on-site and centralized monitoring, or, where justified, centralized monitoring. The sponsor should document the rationale for the chosen monitoring strategy (e.g., in the monitoring plan)."*
- **ICH E6(R2) Section 5.18.2** — the counterweight: *"In general there is a need for on-site monitoring, before, during, and after the trial; however, in exceptional circumstances the sponsor may determine that central monitoring in conjunction with procedures such as investigators' training and meetings, and extensive written guidance can assure appropriate conduct of the trial in accordance with GCP."*
- **ICH E6(R2) Section 5.18.4** — requires a trial-specific monitoring plan describing the strategy, responsibilities, methods, and rationale, emphasizing monitoring of critical data and processes.

### Monitor's responsibilities for verifying data at sites

- **ICH E6(R2) Section 5.18.6** lists the monitor's core duties, which include:
  - verifying that the investigator follows the approved protocol and amendments;
  - verifying that written informed consent was obtained before each subject's participation;
  - checking the accuracy and completeness of CRF entries, source documents, and other trial-related records against each other;
  - verifying that all AEs and SAEs are appropriately reported;
  - verifying that the investigator maintains adequate trial records and provides required reports, notifications, and submissions.
- **ICH E6(R2) Section 5.18.7** requires a written monitoring report after each trial-site visit **or trial-related communication** — the latter phrase is what makes remote/centralized monitoring reporting-compliant.

### Exceptions and conditions

1. **"Where justified" is the gating condition.** The sponsor must articulate *why* centralized-only is adequate for this specific trial. For a Phase III oncology RCT, the justification typically rests on: high data volume, electronic data capture with remote source access, standardized endpoints, and a robust risk assessment.
2. **Risk-based approach is mandatory, not optional.** Section 5.18.3 requires a systematic, prioritized, risk-based approach regardless of modality.
3. **Critical data and processes must still be monitored** (Section 5.18.4). If key efficacy or safety data cannot be verified remotely, some on-site or hybrid activity may be needed to satisfy 5.18.2's "assure appropriate conduct" standard.
4. **Source data verification (SDV) can be remote** only where source documents are accessible electronically or via secure remote review. If source is paper-only and not scanned, centralized-only monitoring may be difficult to defend.
5. **Documentation is the safeguard.** The monitoring plan (5.18.4) and the documented rationale (5.18.3) are what convert a permissible-but-aggressive strategy into a defensible one.

### Practical conclusion

Centralized-only monitoring is **permitted under R2**, but it is not the default. The sponsor should expect regulators (FDA, EMA) to scrutinize the written justification, the risk assessment, and how critical data verification is achieved without site visits. A hybrid approach is often the lower-risk regulatory position; pure centralized-only is defensible for a large, EDC-heavy oncology trial with strong remote data access.

---

## Question 2: Investigator's responsibilities for obtaining informed consent under ICH E6(R2)

### Requirement

The investigator (or a designated person) bears primary responsibility for obtaining **freely given, documented, and properly witnessed** informed consent, in compliance with GCP, applicable regulations, and the Declaration of Helsinki. Section 4.8 governs this in full.

### Citations (Section 4.8)

- **4.8.1** — Investigator must comply with applicable regulatory requirements, adhere to GCP and Helsinki principles, and obtain IRB/IEC written approval of the consent form and any written information **before** trial initiation.
- **4.8.2** — The consent form and written information must be **revised whenever important new information** becomes available that may affect willingness to continue; revisions require IRB/IEC approval in advance of use.
- **4.8.3** — Neither investigator nor staff may **coerce or unduly influence** a subject to participate or continue.
- **4.8.4** — Consent form and written information must be in a **language understandable** to the subject or legally acceptable representative (LAR).
- **4.8.5** — Before consent is obtained, the investigator or designee must give the subject/LAR **ample time and opportunity** to inquire and decide; all questions must be answered to their satisfaction.
- **4.8.6** — The consent form must be **signed and personally dated** by the subject or LAR, and by the person who conducted the consent discussion.
- **4.8.7** — If the subject or LAR is **unable to read**, an **impartial witness** must be present throughout the discussion and must sign and date the form, attesting that information was accurately explained and apparently understood.
- **4.8.10** — The consent form must contain the required **elements (a)–(t)**, including trial purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, alternatives, compensation, confidentiality, and the right to withdraw.
- **4.8.11** — The investigator must provide the subject/LAR with a **copy of the signed and dated consent form** and any other written information.
- **4.8.14** — Where **biological specimens** are collected, consent must address their storage and future use.
- **4.8.15** — Where a subject is enrolled with an LAR, or where the subject regains capacity, **repeat consent** may be required.

### Exceptions and conditions

1. **Legally acceptable representative (LAR).** Where a subject cannot consent (e.g., impaired capacity), consent may be obtained from an LAR, subject to IRB/IEC-approved procedures (see 4.8.8, 4.8.12, 4.8.13 — exact numbering for the LAR-specific paragraphs should be verified against the current R2 text).
2. **Emergency settings.** Consent may be obtained after enrollment where permitted by the protocol and IRB/IEC, with subsequent full consent obtained as soon as feasible.
3. **Illiterate subjects.** The impartial-witness mechanism (4.8.7) is the exception pathway — it does not waive consent, it re-documents it.
4. **Non-therapeutic trials.** Consent requirements may be modified for non-therapeutic trials, but the core elements remain.
5. **Delegation.** The investigator may designate a qualified person to conduct the consent discussion, but the investigator retains overall responsibility.

---

## Cross-reference: ICH E6(R3) (2023)

If the CRO is designing a plan intended to remain current, note that **R3 supersedes R2** and elevates risk-based quality management and centralized monitoring from a permissive option to a more explicit expectation. R3's Section 3 (Quality Management) and Section 5 (Sponsor) reframe monitoring around critical-to-quality factors. A monitoring plan built strictly to R2 may need updating for R3 compliance.

---

## Verification flags

The following citations are stated with high confidence: **5.18.2, 5.18.3, 5.18.4, 5.18.6, 5.18.7, 4.8.1–4.8.7, 4.8.10, 4.8.11, 4.8.14, 4.8.15.** The exact paragraph numbers for the LAR-specific consent provisions (4.8.8, 4.8.9, 4.8.12, 4.8.13) and the emergency-consent provision should be **verified against the current R2 PDF**, as R2 renumbered several paragraphs relative to R1 and the LAR paragraphs are easy to misattribute.

# 7-Day MVP Plan: AI Contract Review Assistant

**Team:** 3 full-stack engineers with clear ownership lanes.
- **Eng A (Backend):** API, auth, DB, jobs, storage.
- **Eng B (Frontend):** Next.js app, review UX, report views.
- **Eng C (AI/Infra):** parsing, LLM pipeline, deployment, observability.

**Stack spine:** Python 3.12 / FastAPI · Next.js 14 (App Router) / TypeScript / Tailwind / shadcn/ui · PostgreSQL 16 + pgvector · Redis · S3-compatible storage · Claude Sonnet 4.5 (primary LLM) + a small model for classification.

---

## 1. System Architecture

```
[Browser: Next.js]
      │ HTTPS (JWT)
      ▼
[API Gateway: FastAPI on Fly.io]
      │
      ├──► [Postgres (Supabase)] ── RLS, tenant isolation
      ├──► [Redis (Upstash)] ── job queue + cache
      ├──► [Object Storage (R2/S3)] ── raw PDFs/DOCX
      └──► [Worker Pool (Celery, Fly Machines)]
                 │
                 ├─► Parser (PyMuPDF / python-docx / Tesseract OCR)
                 ├─► Clause Extractor (LLM, structured output)
                 ├─► Risk Classifier (rules + LLM)
                 ├─► Redline Generator (LLM + playbook RAG via pgvector)
                 └─► Report Synthesizer (LLM → HTML/PDF)
```

**Data flow:** User uploads → API stores raw file in R2, creates `contract` row, enqueues `parse` job → worker extracts text + layout → enqueues `analyze` job → pipeline runs clause extraction → classification → risk scoring → redline generation → report synthesis → writes results to Postgres → frontend polls/subscribes (SSE) for status → renders review UI.

Long jobs are async. The API never blocks on LLM calls. Status is streamed to the client via Server-Sent Events.

---

## 2. Database Schema (Postgres)

```sql
organizations(id uuid pk, name text, plan text, created_at timestamptz)

users(id uuid pk, email citext unique, name text, created_at timestamptz)

memberships(id uuid pk, org_id fk, user_id fk, role text check (role in
  ('owner','admin','reviewer','viewer')), unique(org_id,user_id))

contracts(id uuid pk, org_id fk, title text, counterparty text,
  status text check (status in ('uploaded','parsing','analyzing','ready','failed')),
  file_key text, file_type text, page_count int, created_by fk,
  created_at timestamptz, updated_at timestamptz)

contract_text(id uuid pk, contract_id fk, page int, section text,
  content text, char_start int, char_end int)

clauses(id uuid pk, contract_id fk, clause_type text, heading text,
  text text, page int, char_start int, char_end int,
  confidence numeric, embedding vector(1536))

risks(id uuid pk, clause_id fk, contract_id fk, severity text check
  (severity in ('low','medium','high','critical')), category text,
  rationale text, playbook_ref text, confidence numeric)

redlines(id uuid pk, clause_id fk, original_text text, proposed_text text,
  rationale text, status text check (status in ('proposed','accepted','rejected')),
  created_at timestamptz)

reports(id uuid pk, contract_id fk, summary text, risk_counts jsonb,
  html text, pdf_key text, generated_at timestamptz)

playbook_rules(id uuid pk, org_id fk, clause_type text, rule text,
  preferred_language text, embedding vector(1536))

jobs(id uuid pk, contract_id fk, type text, status text, attempts int,
  error text, created_at timestamptz, finished_at timestamptz)

audit_logs(id uuid pk, org_id fk, user_id fk, action text, target text,
  metadata jsonb, created_at timestamptz)

api_keys(id uuid pk, org_id fk, hashed_key text, last_used timestamptz)
```

Indexes on `contracts(org_id, status)`, `clauses(contract_id)`, `risks(contract_id, severity)`, and an HNSW index on `clauses.embedding` and `playbook_rules.embedding`. Row-Level Security policies keyed on `org_id` from the JWT claim enforce tenant isolation at the DB layer.

---

## 3. Backend API Endpoints

All under `/v1`, JSON, JWT bearer auth.

| Method | Path | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| POST | `/contracts` | Upload (multipart) → returns contract + upload URL |
| GET | `/contracts` | List (paginated, filter by status) |
| GET | `/contracts/{id}` | Get contract + status |
| GET | `/contracts/{id}/stream` | SSE status stream |
| POST | `/contracts/{id}/analyze` | Trigger pipeline |
| GET | `/contracts/{id}/clauses` | Extracted clauses |
| GET | `/contracts/{id}/risks` | Risks |
| GET | `/contracts/{id}/report` | Summary report (HTML/JSON) |
| PATCH | `/redlines/{id}` | Edit proposed redline |
| POST | `/redlines/{id}/accept` | Accept redline |
| POST | `/redlines/{id}/reject` | Reject redline |
| GET | `/playbook` / POST | List/create rules |
| GET | `/orgs/{id}/members` | Team management |

**Example — POST /contracts**
```json
// request (multipart): file=@msa.pdf, title="Acme MSA"
// response 201
{ "id": "c_8f2a", "status": "uploaded",
  "upload_url": "https://r2.../signed" }
```

**Example — GET /contracts/{id}/risks**
```json
{ "contract_id": "c_8f2a", "risks": [
  { "id": "r_1", "clause_id": "cl_9", "severity": "high",
    "category": "indemnification", "rationale": "Uncapped indemnity...",
    "confidence": 0.91 } ] }
```

**Example — POST /redlines/{id}/accept**
```json
{ "id": "rl_3", "status": "accepted", "updated_at": "2026-10-09T12:00:00Z" }
```

---

## 4. Authentication & Authorization

- **Auth:** Supabase Auth (email/password + magic link). Issues short-lived JWTs (15 min) with refresh tokens. JWT carries `sub` (user), `org_id`, `role`.
- **Authorization:** RBAC at the API layer + Postgres RLS as defense-in-depth. Roles: `owner` > `admin` > `reviewer` > `viewer`. Only `admin`+ can invite/delete; `reviewer`+ can edit redlines; `viewer` is read-only.
- **Tenant isolation:** Every query scoped by `org_id`; RLS policies enforce it even if the API forgets.
- **API keys:** For future integrations — hashed (bcrypt) in `api_keys`, scoped to org.
- **Transport:** TLS everywhere; files in R2 via signed URLs (5-min expiry).

---

## 5. Frontend Screens & Navigation

```
/login
/dashboard            → contract list, status chips, upload CTA
/contracts/new        → drag-drop upload, title/counterparty
/contracts/[id]       → split view: document (left) + clause/risk sidebar (right)
                        tabs: Clauses | Risks | Redlines | Report
/contracts/[id]/report→ printable summary, export PDF
/playbook             → org rule editor
/settings/team        → members, roles, invites
```

Key UX: the review screen is a **split-pane** — PDF viewer (react-pdf) on the left with clause highlights, and a right rail listing clauses color-coded by severity. Clicking a risk scrolls the doc to the clause. Redlines show a diff (original vs proposed) with Accept/Reject/Edit. A top progress bar reflects SSE pipeline status. Built with shadcn/ui + Tailwind; state via TanStack Query.

---

## 6. AI/LLM Pipeline

**Stage 0 — Parse.** PyMuPDF for text+coordinates; `python-docx` for Word; Tesseract OCR fallback when text layer is missing. Output: page-tagged text with char offsets.

**Stage 1 — Section & clause extraction.** Chunk by headings + sliding window (2k tokens, 200 overlap). Send each chunk to Claude Sonnet 4.5 with a **structured-output tool schema** returning `{clause_type, heading, text, char_start, char_end, confidence}`. Clause taxonomy is a fixed enum (indemnification, limitation_of_liability, termination, governing_law, IP, confidentiality, payment, etc.).

**Stage 2 — Classification.** Map extracted clauses to the taxonomy using a cheap model (Claude Haiku) with few-shot examples; cache by text hash.

**Stage 3 — Risk scoring.** Hybrid: deterministic rules (e.g., "indemnity uncapped" → high) + LLM judgment against the org's playbook. Playbook rules retrieved via pgvector similarity (RAG). Output: severity, category, rationale, confidence.

**Stage 4 — Redline generation.** For each high/critical risk, prompt the LLM with the clause + matched playbook preferred language → proposed replacement text + rationale. Structured output; diff computed client-side.

**Stage 5 — Report synthesis.** Aggregate risk counts + clause summaries → LLM writes an executive summary → render to HTML → PDF (WeasyPrint).

**Guardrails:** every LLM call uses tool/JSON schemas, temperature 0, and a confidence threshold (below 0.6 → flagged "needs human review"). All prompts versioned in code. Langfuse traces every call (tokens, latency, cost).

---

## 7. Deployment Stack & Infrastructure

| Layer | Service |
|---|---|
| Frontend | Vercel (Next.js) |
| API + workers | Fly.io (FastAPI + Celery, separate machine groups, autoscale) |
| Database | Supabase Postgres 16 + pgvector |
| Queue/cache | Upstash Redis |
| File storage | Cloudflare R2 (S3-compatible) |
| Auth | Supabase Auth |
| LLM | Anthropic API (Sonnet 4.5 + Haiku) |
| PDF render | WeasyPrint in worker |
| Secrets | Fly secrets / Doppler |
| CI/CD | GitHub Actions → Fly deploy + Vercel preview |

IaC via a single `fly.toml` + Supabase migrations (Alembic). Staging and prod environments separated.

---

## 8. Observability, Logging, Error Handling

- **Errors:** Sentry (frontend + backend) with release tagging. Global FastAPI exception handler returns RFC-7807 problem+json.
- **Logs:** structured JSON to stdout → shipped to Axiom. Every request has a `trace_id` propagated to workers.
- **LLM tracing:** Langfuse — per-call tokens, latency, cost, prompt version.
- **Metrics:** Fly metrics + a `/health` and `/ready` endpoint; Grafana dashboard for p95 latency, job failure rate, LLM cost/day.
- **Job resilience:** Celery retries with exponential backoff (max 3), dead-letter queue, `jobs.error` persisted, user-visible "failed, retry" button.
- **Alerts:** Sentry alert rules + a Slack webhook for job failure rate > 5% and LLM spend > daily threshold.
- **Audit:** every mutation writes to `audit_logs`.

---

## 9. Day-by-Day 7-Day Schedule

**Day 1 — Foundations.** Repo, CI, environments. Supabase project + schema + RLS. Auth flow end-to-end. Upload endpoint + R2 signed URLs. *Deliverable: login + upload a file.*

**Day 2 — Parsing + extraction.** Parser worker (PDF/DOCX/OCR). Clause extraction with structured output. `clauses` persisted. SSE status stream. *Deliverable: upload → clauses listed.*

**Day 3 — Risk + redlines.** Classification, risk rules + LLM scoring, playbook table + RAG retrieval, redline generation. *Deliverable: risks + proposed redlines.*

**Day 4 — Review UI.** Split-pane document viewer, clause/risk sidebar, redline diff + accept/reject. *Deliverable: full review screen.*

**Day 5 — Report + playbook + team.** Report synthesis + PDF export. Playbook editor. Team/roles screens. *Deliverable: end-to-end flow complete.*

**Day 6 — Hardening.** Sentry, Langfuse, logging, retries, RLS tests, load test with 20 concurrent contracts, cost instrumentation. *Deliverable: observability + reliability.*

**Day 7 — Ship.** Staging→prod deploy, seed demo data, polish empty/error states, runbook, demo script, buffer. *Deliverable: live MVP + demo.*

---

## 10. Cost Estimate @ 100 Active Users/Month

Assume 10 contracts/user/month = **1,000 contracts/month**, ~30 pages each.

| Item | Monthly |
|---|---|
| LLM (Sonnet extraction/redlines ~$0.25/contract, Haiku classification ~$0.03) | ~$280 |
| Embeddings (pgvector, OpenAI/Anthropic) | ~$15 |
| Supabase Pro | $25 |
| Fly.io (API + workers) | ~$60 |
| Upstash Redis | ~$15 |
| Cloudflare R2 (storage + egress) | ~$10 |
| Vercel Pro | $20 |
| Sentry + Axiom + Langfuse | ~$50 |
| **Total** | **~$475/month** |

Dominant cost is LLM tokens. Levers: cache clause classifications by hash, use Haiku for classification, batch extraction, cap contract page length on the free tier.

---

## 11. Top 5 Technical Risks & Mitigations

1. **LLM hallucination in clause extraction.** → Structured-output schemas, temperature 0, confidence threshold, char-offset grounding so every clause maps to real text, human review flag.
2. **PDF parsing failures (scanned/odd layouts).** → Multi-parser chain with OCR fallback, layout-aware extraction, "paste text manually" escape hatch, parse-failure alerting.
3. **Latency & cost blowup.** → Async workers, parallel chunk processing, model tiering (Haiku for classification), response caching, per-org spend caps.
4. **Data privacy for legal docs.** → Tenant RLS, encryption at rest, signed short-lived URLs, zero-retention LLM config, audit logs, org-level data deletion.
5. **7-day scope creep.** → Frozen feature list, feature flags, "needs human review" instead of perfect automation, daily demo to catch drift, Day 7 reserved as buffer.

---

## 12. Explicitly Out of MVP Scope

- E-signature / DocuSign integration.
- Multi-round negotiation tracking & version diffing beyond basic.
- Custom playbook builder UI (rules seeded via config, editable as text).
- SSO/SAML, SCIM provisioning.
- Non-English contracts.
- Mobile app.
- Third-party integrations (Salesforce, Slack, Google Drive).
- Fine-tuned models (prompting only).
- On-prem / VPC deployment.
- Clause-level collaboration (comments, mentions).
- Advanced analytics dashboards.
- Bulk/batch upload beyond single-file.

---

**Build order recap:** auth → upload → parse → extract → risk → redline → review UI → report → harden → ship. Everything async, everything tenant-isolated, everything traced. Ship the happy path; flag the rest.

Happy to help. Before locking anything in, here's my read on the situation plus the questions I need answered.

**My preliminary take:** Notification overload and duplicate work usually travel together, and the root cause is typically Slack being used as both a chat tool *and* a de facto project tracker — which it's terrible at. When assignments, decisions, and status live buried in channels, people miss things, redo each other's work, and get pinged constantly to compensate. The fix is usually separating "where work lives" from "where people talk," either through a lightweight process change (single source of truth + notification hygiene) or a small custom build (e.g., a bot that consolidates assignments and flags duplicates, or a dashboard that aggregates what everyone's working on).

**Clarifying questions:**

1. What does "duplicate work" actually look like for you — two people unknowingly doing the same task, the same discussions happening in multiple channels, or work being redone because context got lost?
2. How big is the team, and how is it structured (one team, several sub-teams, cross-functional)?
3. What tools do you currently use to track work — Jira, Linear, Asana, spreadsheets, or is Slack itself the tracker?
4. Is the bigger pain the raw notification volume, or the interruptions breaking people's focus?
5. When you say "built" — are you specifically looking for a custom app/bot, or would you be equally happy with configuring existing tools if that solves it?
6. How does work currently get assigned to people — Slack threads, meetings, email, something else?

Once I know these, I can tell you whether you need something actually built (and what) or whether this is mostly a process and configuration problem — which is cheaper and faster to fix.

# Drug Interaction Review

**Patient regimen:** warfarin 5 mg daily (AF) + ibuprofen 400 mg TID PRN (OA pain) + lisinopril 10 mg daily (HTN)

---

## Pair 1: Warfarin + Ibuprofen — **Major**

**Mechanism (multiple, predominantly pharmacodynamic):**
- **Additive bleeding risk:** Warfarin inhibits VKORC1, reducing synthesis of functional clotting factors II, VII, IX, X. Ibuprofen reversibly inhibits platelet COX-1, reducing thromboxane A2 and impairing platelet aggregation. The combination produces anticoagulant + antiplatelet synergy.
- **GI mucosal injury:** COX-1 inhibition reduces gastric prostaglandin (PGE2/PGI2)-mediated cytoprotection (mucus, bicarbonate, mucosal blood flow), creating erosions/ulcers. Anticoagulation then amplifies the severity of any GI bleed.
- **Minor pharmacokinetic contribution:** Both drugs are >99% protein-bound; displacement of warfarin transiently raises the free fraction, but this normalizes with redistribution and is of limited clinical importance. Ibuprofen is primarily a CYP2C9 *substrate*; weak competitive inhibition of CYP2C9 (the enzyme that clears the more potent S-warfarin enantiomer) has been described, but the evidence is inconsistent and the pharmacodynamic interaction dominates. I flag this as a component of uncertain clinical significance rather than a driver.

**Clinical action:**
- Preferred: substitute **acetaminophen** as first-line analgesic (note: sustained high doses, e.g., >2 g/day for several days, can itself potentiate warfarin via effects on the vitamin K cycle and CYP2C9 competition — keep doses moderate).
- If ibuprofen is necessary: use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, add a **PPI** for GI prophylaxis, intensify INR monitoring (e.g., recheck within 3–5 days of starting regular use), and counsel on bleeding signs (melena, hematuria, excessive bruising).
- Since ibuprofen's antiplatelet effect is reversible (unlike aspirin), it cannot be mitigated by timing separation.

*Classification note:* some references rate this pair as moderate because ibuprofen is among the "safer" NSAIDs with warfarin, but given the AF indication and GI hemorrhage risk, treating it as major is the safer clinical posture.

---

## Pair 2: Warfarin + Lisinopril — **No established clinically significant interaction**

There is no well-documented, reproducible interaction between these agents. Scattered case reports of ACE inhibitor–associated INR elevation exist, but the evidence is insufficient to constitute an established interaction. **No intervention beyond routine INR monitoring is warranted.** I state this explicitly rather than inventing a theoretical mechanism.

---

## Pair 3: Ibuprofen + Lisinopril — **Moderate**

**Mechanism (pharmacodynamic, renal hemodynamic + electrolyte):**
- **AKI risk:** Lisinopril reduces angiotensin II, dilating the efferent arteriole and lowering glomerular capillary pressure. Ibuprofen inhibits renal prostaglandin synthesis, constricting the afferent arteriole and reducing renal blood flow. The combination creates a "double hit" on glomerular filtration. (The classic "triple whammy" requires a diuretic, which this patient is not on — but baseline risk remains.)
- **Blunted antihypertensive effect:** NSAID-mediated sodium and water retention (reduced prostaglandin-dependent natriuresis) antagonizes ACE inhibitor blood pressure control.
- **Additive hyperkalemia:** NSAIDs suppress renin release (→ ↓aldosterone) and ACE inhibitors directly reduce aldosterone; effects on potassium are additive.

**Clinical action:**
- Monitor blood pressure, serum creatinine/eGFR, and potassium if ibuprofen is used regularly.
- Ensure adequate hydration; limit duration of NSAID use.
- Again, acetaminophen or a **topical NSAID** (minimal systemic absorption) is preferred for osteoarthritis.

---

## Overall Assessment

The **warfarin + ibuprofen pair is the dominant clinical concern** in this regimen — major bleeding risk that is compounded by the concurrent lisinopril (renal vulnerability). The single most impactful intervention is replacing ibuprofen with acetaminophen. If NSAID therapy is unavoidable, add a PPI, tighten INR monitoring, and check renal function and potassium within 1–2 weeks of regular use.

# MVP Plan: AI Contract Review Assistant ("ClauseGuard" — working name)

**Team:** E1 (backend/infra), E2 (AI pipeline), E3 (frontend)
**Stack summary:** Next.js + TypeScript frontend on Vercel · Python 3.12 / FastAPI backend + Celery workers on Fly.io · Neon Postgres · Upstash Redis · AWS S3 · Anthropic Claude API

---

## 1. System Architecture

**Components:**

1. **Web app (Next.js 14, TypeScript, Tailwind, shadcn/ui)** — served on Vercel. Handles auth UI, upload, review workspace, report viewing.
2. **API service (FastAPI, Python 3.12)** — REST API, JWT auth, org-scoped RBAC, presigned S3 upload URLs, job orchestration. Stateless, horizontally scalable.
3. **Worker service (Celery on same FastAPI codebase, separate Docker image entrypoint)** — consumes jobs from Upstash Redis: document parsing, clause extraction, risk classification, redline generation, report generation.
4. **Document parser module** — PyMuPDF (PDF text), python-docx (.docx), AWS Textract fallback for scanned/image PDFs.
5. **AI pipeline module** — Anthropic Claude (claude-sonnet-4-5) with tool-use/structured JSON outputs; Pydantic-validated schemas; prompt caching.
6. **Postgres (Neon)** — all application data. **S3** — raw contract files (private bucket, SSE-KMS). **Redis (Upstash)** — Celery broker + result backend.
7. **PDF/report renderer** — WeasyPrint for summary PDF generation.

**Data flow (happy path):**

```
User → [1] Next.js upload UI
     → [2] POST /contracts → API creates contract row (status=uploaded), returns presigned S3 URL
     → client PUTs file to S3 → client POST /contracts/{id}/analyze
     → [3] API enqueues Celery job → worker:
         a. Downloads from S3, parses to text + page/char offsets
         b. Chunks by structure (~3k tokens, overlap)
         c. Claude: clause extraction (structured JSON) → clauses table
         d. Playbook rules + Claude: risk classification → risks table
         e. Claude: redline suggestions for medium/high risks → redlines table
         f. Claude: aggregate summary report + risk score → reports table
         g. contract.status = complete
     → [4] Frontend polls GET /contracts/{id}/status (2s interval) → renders workspace
     → User reviews, accepts/rejects redlines, exports summary PDF
```

Failures at any worker step: job retried (max 3, exponential backoff), then `status=failed` with error surfaced in UI; contract can be re-analyzed.

## 6. AI/LLM Pipeline

**Model:** Anthropic Claude (`claude-sonnet-4-5`) via official Python SDK, temperature 0, tool-use forced JSON outputs, prompt caching enabled for the static system prompt + playbook.

**Stage 0 — Parsing:** PyMuPDF extracts text with page numbers; python-docx for .docx; if PDF text density < threshold (likely scanned), route through AWS Textract. Store char offsets so every clause links back to its location in the document.

**Stage 1 — Chunking:** Structure-aware splitting on headings/paragraph boundaries, target ~3,000 tokens/chunk, 200-token overlap. SHA-256 hash per chunk for caching (re-analysis of same doc skips identical chunks).

**Stage 2 — Clause extraction:** Per chunk, Claude with a tool schema:
```json
{ "clauses": [ { "clause_type": "<from 20-type taxonomy>", "title": "...",
    "text": "<verbatim>", "page_start": 0, "page_end": 0,
    "confidence": 0.0 } ] }
```
Taxonomy (~20 types): payment terms, term & termination, auto-renewal, limitation of liability, indemnification, IP ownership, license scope, confidentiality, non-solicit, non-compete, governing law, dispute resolution, warranties, insurance, force majeure, assignment, data protection, SLA, pricing/fees, audit rights.

**Stage 3 — Risk classification (hybrid):** First, deterministic playbook rules (regex/keyword + logic, e.g., "liability section present but no cap" → high; "auto-renewal without termination window" → medium). Clauses not resolved by rules go to Claude with a severity rubric prompt (high = material financial/legal exposure; medium = unfavorable but negotiable; low = deviation from market standard), outputting `{severity, category, description, rationale, quote, confidence}`. Every risk must quote verbatim text from the clause — quote mismatch → retry once, then downgrade confidence.

**Stage 4 — Redline generation:** For medium/high risks only. Few-shot prompt with 3 worked examples per category; output `{suggested_text, rationale}`. Style constraint in prompt: preserve defined-term references and contract voice.

**Stage 5 — Report:** Single Claude call aggregating stored clauses/risks → executive summary (markdown), top-5 risks, recommendations. Risk score = weighted sum (high=10, medium=5, low=2) normalized to 0–10.

**Reliability guardrails:** Pydantic validation on every LLM response; 2 retries with backoff on schema failure; per-contract token budget cap (250k tokens) with graceful degradation (skip redlines for low-severity items); all model version + token usage persisted in `reports.token_usage` for cost tracking. **Golden test set:** 15 annotated sample contracts run nightly in CI — extraction F1 and risk precision must not regress.

## 1. Centralized-Only Monitoring Under ICH E6(R2)

**Requirement:** Yes, ICH E6(R2) permits a centralized-only monitoring approach, provided the sponsor can demonstrate that on-site visits are not necessary to ensure trial quality and data integrity. Centralized monitoring is explicitly endorsed as part of a risk-based monitoring strategy.

**Key citations:**

- **ICH E6(R2) Section 5.18.3 (Monitoring – Extent and Nature):** The determination of the extent and nature of monitoring should be "risk-based" and consider factors such as trial complexity, endpoints, and the experience of the investigator. Notably, E6(R2) added the statement that monitoring should include **"a combination of on-site and centralized monitoring activities"** — but the guideline also states that **"centralized monitoring processes can provide additional value"** and that sponsors may justify alternative approaches. The exact wording acknowledges centralized monitoring as a legitimate, sometimes sufficient, complement or partial substitute for on-site visits.
- **Section 5.18.7 (Risk-Based Monitoring, added in R2):** Sponsors should develop a systematic, prioritized, risk-based monitoring strategy. The guideline states that on-site monitoring may be reduced in frequency or scope where centralized monitoring shows adequate control of site performance and data quality.

**Conditions/exceptions:**
- The sponsor must document the rationale for the monitoring approach in the monitoring plan.
- The monitor's core responsibilities under **Section 5.18.4 (Monitor Responsibilities)** still apply — including verifying that data are accurate, complete, and verifiable against source documents. The guideline says the monitor should verify source data "at the investigative site" — historically interpreted as requiring on-site source data verification (SDV). A centralized-only plan must therefore address how source data verification will be achieved remotely (e.g., remote access to EHR/EMR systems, certified copies, or reliance on statistical/centralized checks with reduced SDV).
- **Section 4.9 (Records and Reports / investigator source data obligations)** and **Section 8.x** requirements for source documentation remain — the investigator must still maintain adequate and accurate source records regardless of monitoring method.
- Regulatory authorities (e.g., FDA, EMA) have accepted centralized-only plans, but inspectors may still question the plan if data integrity cannot be demonstrated. Note that **ICH E6(R3)** (adopted 2025, rolling out) further strengthens the acceptability of decentralized and centralized monitoring approaches.

**Practical caveat:** For a Phase III oncology trial, expect scrutiny of how source verification, drug accountability (Section 5.14), and site qualification (Section 5.18.2) are handled without on-site visits. A fully centralized plan is defensible but must be robustly justified.

## 2. Investigator's Responsibilities for Informed Consent Under ICH E6(R2)

**Requirement:** The investigator (or a delegated, qualified designee per institutional requirements) must obtain freely given informed consent from every trial subject (or their legally acceptable representative) before any trial-related procedures are performed, using a current IRB/IEC-approved consent form.

**Key citations:**

- **Section 4.8.1:** The investigator must conduct the trial in compliance with the protocol agreed to by the sponsor and IRB/IEC, including informed consent requirements.
- **Section 4.8.2:** Freely given informed consent must be obtained from every subject **prior to participation**. For subjects with a legal representative (relevant in oncology — e.g., impaired capacity patients), consent comes from the legally acceptable representative, and the subject's assent should be sought where capable.
- **Section 4.8.3:** Both the informed consent discussion and the written consent document must include the elements described in **Section 4.8.10** and comply with applicable regulatory requirements. Neither the subject nor the representative may waive legal rights.
- **Section 4.8.4:** The consent document must be in language understandable to the subject, and time for questions and consideration must be allowed.
- **Section 4.8.5:** Before the trial begins, the investigator must have the IRB/IEC's written approval of the written informed consent form and any other written information provided to subjects, plus any updates.
- **Section 4.8.7:** Before participation, the subject or representative must be informed of all pertinent aspects of the trial, including the IRB/IEC approval of the trial.
- **Section 4.8.8:** If new information becomes available that may affect consent, the revised written information and consent form must be approved by the IRB/IEC and communicated to ongoing subjects.
- **Section 4.8.9:** Consent must be documented by a **dated, personally signed and initialed** form by the subject or representative and the person conducting the consent discussion.
- **Section 4.8.10:** Enumerates the required content elements (trial purpose, procedures, duration, risks/benefits, alternatives, confidentiality, compensation/medical treatment for injury, contacts, voluntary participation, and consequences of withdrawal).
- **Section 4.8.11:** Non-therapeutic trials require consent per 4.8.10 and, where required, per 4.8.12.
- **Section 4.8.12:** Special protections for vulnerable subjects in emergency situations (e.g., consent not possible, life-threatening situation, no alternative treatment of equal chance of survival).

**Conditions/exceptions:**
- Consent may be obtained by a designee, but the investigator retains overall responsibility and must ensure the designee is qualified and properly delegated (Section 4.2.5/4.8).
- In emergency situations, the exceptions in 4.8.12 may apply (subject to IRB/IEC and regulatory approval).
- For oncology trials, special attention to subjects with impaired decision-making capacity and to re-consent upon protocol amendments or new safety information.

**Verification note:** Section numbers above reflect ICH E6(R2) as adopted in 2016; they are stable and well-established, but if drafting regulatory submissions, verify against the current official ICH E6 guideline text, as E6(R3) is now supplanting R2 in some jurisdictions.

Here are the 3 pairwise interactions from this list:

### 1. Warfarin + Ibuprofen
1. **Interacting pair:** Warfarin 5 mg daily + Ibuprofen 400 mg TID PRN
2. **Severity:** Major
3. **Mechanism:** Primarily pharmacodynamic synergy, not a major pharmacokinetic interaction. Ibuprofen reversibly inhibits platelet COX-1, impairing platelet aggregation and primary hemostasis, while warfarin inhibits vitamin K-dependent clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X. Ibuprofen also inhibits gastric prostaglandin synthesis, causing mucosal erosion/ulceration that creates a bleeding site. Ibuprofen is a CYP2C9 substrate (the main enzyme for S-warfarin) and can weakly compete in vitro, but this is not considered the clinically dominant mechanism for INR elevation.
4. **Recommended action:** Avoid the combination, especially chronic or regular PRN use. Switch osteoarthritis pain to acetaminophen, topical diclofenac, physical therapy, or other non-NSAID measures. If an oral NSAID is absolutely unavoidable, use the lowest dose for the shortest duration, add a PPI for GI protection, counsel on bleeding signs (melena, hematuria, unusual bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding), and check INR 3-5 days after starting, stopping, or changing the ibuprofen dose.

### 2. Ibuprofen + Lisinopril
1. **Interacting pair:** Ibuprofen 400 mg TID PRN + Lisinopril 10 mg daily
2. **Severity:** Moderate - Major in older adults, CKD, volume depletion, or heart failure
3. **Mechanism:** Pharmacodynamic antagonism at the kidney. Lisinopril blocks angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction. Ibuprofen inhibits COX-1/COX-2 prostaglandin synthesis (PGE2, PGI2), removing prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar vasodilation. Together this drops glomerular filtration pressure and GFR. NSAID-mediated sodium and water retention also blunts the antihypertensive effect of lisinopril. Both drugs increase hyperkalemia risk - lisinopril by reducing aldosterone, ibuprofen by reducing renin and renal potassium excretion.
4. **Recommended action:** Avoid chronic ibuprofen. Monitor blood pressure, serum creatinine/eGFR, and potassium within 1-2 weeks of starting regular ibuprofen and after dose changes (earlier, 3-7 days, if high risk). Counsel to maintain hydration and to hold/seek care during acute illness with dehydration. Use acetaminophen or topical therapy for osteoarthritis instead.

### 3. Warfarin + Lisinopril
1. **Interacting pair:** Warfarin 5 mg daily + Lisinopril 10 mg daily
2. **Severity:** Minor / No clinically significant interaction established
3. **Mechanism:** No established CYP or pharmacodynamic mechanism. Lisinopril is not metabolized by CYP enzymes and is excreted unchanged in urine, so it does not inhibit or induce CYP2C9, CYP1A2, or CYP3A4 - the enzymes that clear S- and R-warfarin. I am uncertain about isolated case reports of INR changes after starting ACE inhibitors because a causal mechanism has not been demonstrated; changes are more likely due to diet, illness, heart failure status, or other drugs.
4. **Recommended action:** No dose adjustment needed for this pair alone. Continue routine INR monitoring, with a routine check after any major change in clinical status, diet, or other medications, as per standard warfarin care.

**Summary priority:** Stop/replace oral ibuprofen - it drives both clinically significant interactions in this regimen.

As a regulatory affairs specialist under ICH E6(R2) Good Clinical Practice, the answers are:

### 1. Centralized-only monitoring without any on-site visits

**1. Requirement clearly stated**
ICH E6(R2) does not permit centralized-only monitoring as a routine default. In general, on-site monitoring is required before, during, and after the trial. Centralized monitoring may complement and reduce the extent and/or frequency of on-site monitoring under a risk-based approach, but eliminating on-site monitoring entirely is only contemplated in exceptional circumstances with documented justification.
For a Phase III oncology trial — high complexity, safety-critical endpoints, investigational product handling, dose modifications, tumor assessments, and serious adverse events — a sponsor would have difficulty justifying no on-site visits on risk grounds alone.

**2. Relevant guideline sections**
- ICH E6(R2) Section 5.18.1 - Purpose of Monitoring: To verify that the rights and well-being of subjects are protected, reported trial data are accurate, complete, and verifiable from source documents, and conduct is in compliance with the protocol, GCP, and applicable regulatory requirements.
- ICH E6(R2) Section 5.18.3 - Extent and Nature of Monitoring: "In general there is a need for on-site monitoring, before, during, and after the trial. However in exceptional circumstances the sponsor may determine that central monitoring in conjunction with procedures such as investigators' training and meetings, and extensive written guidance can assure appropriate conduct of the trial in accordance with GCP. Statistically controlled sampling may be an acceptable method for selecting the data to be verified."
- ICH E6(R2) Section 5.18.3, Addendum (R2): The sponsor should develop a systematic, prioritized, risk-based approach. Centralized monitoring is defined as remote evaluation by sponsor personnel or representatives, and it "can complement and reduce the extent and/or frequency of on-site monitoring" — not automatically replace it.
- ICH E6(R2) Section 5.18.7, Addendum (R2) - Monitoring Plan: The sponsor should develop a monitoring plan tailored to the specific human subject protection and data integrity risks of the trial, describing the strategy, responsibilities, methods, and rationale for the chosen approach.
- ICH E6(R2) Section 5.18.4 - Monitor's Responsibilities: The monitor must, when relevant and necessary: act as the main line of communication between sponsor and investigator (5.18.4(a)); verify adequate investigator qualifications, resources, facilities, and staff (5.18.4(b)-(d)); verify written informed consent was obtained before participation (5.18.4(e)); verify investigational product storage, dispensing, and accountability (5.18.4(f)-(g)); verify the investigator follows the approved protocol and that source documents and trial records are accurate, complete, kept up-to-date, and maintained (5.18.4(h)-(i)); check the accuracy and completeness of CRF entries against source documents (5.18.4(k)-(l)); and determine whether adverse events are appropriately reported and deviations communicated (5.18.4(m)-(n)).

**3. Exceptions or conditions**
- Exceptional circumstances only: Centralized monitoring alone may be acceptable if the sponsor documents why, combined with investigator training/meetings and extensive written guidance, it will assure appropriate conduct.
- Risk-based reduction is allowed: Frequency and extent of on-site visits and source data verification can be reduced, and statistically controlled sampling used, if justified in the monitoring plan based on trial objective, design, complexity, blinding, size, and endpoints under 5.18.3.
- Practical limitation: Several 5.18.4 duties — e.g., verifying source documents, informed consent originals, IP storage/accountability, and site facilities — cannot be fully discharged remotely unless the site uses validated electronic source/eConsent systems with monitor access that satisfies source verification requirements.

### 2. Investigator's responsibilities for obtaining informed consent

**1. Requirement clearly stated**
The investigator must obtain freely given, written informed consent from every subject (or legally acceptable representative) prior to any trial participation, after fully informing them of all pertinent aspects of the trial, using an IRB/IEC-approved consent form and information, in non-technical understandable language, without coercion, and must document it by signed and personally dated consent.

This reflects ICH E6(R2) Principle 2.9 in Section 2: "Freely given informed consent should be obtained from every subject prior to clinical trial participation."

**2. Relevant guideline sections**
- ICH E6(R2) Section 4.8.1: In obtaining and documenting informed consent, the investigator should comply with applicable regulatory requirements and adhere to GCP and the Declaration of Helsinki. Prior to the trial, the investigator should have IRB/IEC written approval/favourable opinion of the written informed consent form and any other written information to be provided.
- ICH E6(R2) Section 4.8.3: Neither the investigator nor trial staff should coerce or unduly influence a subject to participate or continue.
- ICH E6(R2) Section 4.8.4: No oral or written information, including the consent form, should contain language causing the subject or representative to waive legal rights or release the investigator, institution, sponsor, or agents from liability for negligence.
- ICH E6(R2) Section 4.8.5 - 4.8.7: The investigator, or a person designated by the investigator, should fully inform the subject or legally acceptable representative of all pertinent aspects, provide ample time and opportunity to inquire, and answer all questions to the subject's satisfaction before consent is obtained.
- ICH E6(R2) Section 4.8.8: Prior to participation, the written consent form should be signed and personally dated by the subject or legally acceptable representative, and by the person who conducted the consent discussion.
- ICH E6(R2) Section 4.8.10: The discussion and form must include, among other items: that the trial involves research, purpose, treatments and randomization probability, procedures, subject responsibilities, experimental aspects, foreseeable risks and inconveniences, expected benefits, alternative treatments, compensation/treatment for injury, payments and expenses if any, voluntary nature and right to withdraw without penalty, access to records by monitors/auditors/IRB/IEC and regulatory authorities with confidentiality protections, contacts for information and injury, foreseeable circumstances for termination, expected duration, and approximate number of subjects.
- ICH E6(R2) Section 4.8.2 and 4.8.11: Revised consent forms/information require prior IRB/IEC approval (except where necessary to eliminate immediate hazards), and the subject or representative must receive a copy of the signed and dated form and any updates during participation.

**3. Exceptions or conditions**
- Unable to read - Section 4.8.9: An impartial witness must be present during the entire consent discussion; after the form is read and explained and oral consent given, the subject/representative signs/dates if capable, and the witness signs/dates attesting the information was accurately explained and apparently understood.
- Legally acceptable representative - Sections 4.8.12 to 4.8.14: For subjects who can only be enrolled with representative consent (e.g., minors, severe dementia), the subject should still be informed to the extent compatible with their understanding and, if capable, should sign and personally date the consent. Additional conditions apply to non-therapeutic trials conducted with representative consent.
- Emergency situations - Section 4.8.15: When prior consent from the subject is not possible, consent of the legally acceptable representative, if present, should be requested. If neither is available, enrolment may proceed only under measures described in the protocol and/or elsewhere with documented IRB/IEC approval/favourable opinion to protect rights, safety, and well-being; the subject or representative must be informed as soon as possible and consent to continue sought.
- New information - Section 4.8.2: If important new information becomes available that may affect willingness to continue, it must be communicated in a timely manner, documented, and the revised form approved by the IRB/IEC before use, unless necessary to eliminate an immediate hazard.

# AI Contract Review Assistant - 7-Day MVP Build Plan

**Team split:** Engineer A = Frontend Lead, Engineer B = Backend / Infra Lead, Engineer C = AI / Document Pipeline Lead
**Core bet for speed:** TypeScript monorepo, managed services everywhere, no Kubernetes, no custom ML training. Buy auth, DB, queue, and file storage.

## 1. System Architecture

**Stack choice:** Next.js 14 frontend, Node.js Fastify backend API, Python 3.12 worker for document parsing + AI. Shared PostgreSQL database.

Components:
- **Web App:** Next.js 14 App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, hosted on Vercel. Talks only to Backend API via HTTPS.
- **API Service:** Node.js 20, Fastify, Prisma ORM, Zod validation. Stateless, handles auth, CRUD, presigned uploads, job enqueueing.
- **AI Worker:** Python 3.12, FastAPI for health check only + BullMQ consumer pattern via Redis polling in Python using `redis-py`. Separate service because PDF/DOCX parsing libraries are best in Python.
- **Queue / Jobs:** Upstash Redis + BullMQ for Node enqueue, Python worker consumes `contract-processing` queue. Jobs are idempotent by `job_id`.
- **Database:** PostgreSQL 15 on Supabase, accessed via Prisma. Row-level tenant isolation enforced in app layer + Supabase RLS as backup.
- **File Storage:** AWS S3 bucket `contracts-prod` with SSE-KMS encryption. Original files, extracted text artifacts, exported reports stored here. Never store files on disk.
- **LLM Provider:** OpenAI API - GPT-4o-mini for extraction/classification, GPT-4o for redlines/summary.
- **Email:** Resend for invites and processing-complete notifications.

Data flow:
1. User requests upload in Web App -> API returns S3 presigned PUT URL (15 min expiry)
2. Browser uploads PDF/DOCX directly to S3 -> Browser calls `POST /contracts/:id/complete`
3. API creates `processing_jobs` row, enqueues job to Redis
4. Python Worker downloads from S3, extracts text with page/paragraph offsets, segments clauses, calls OpenAI per clause in parallel, saves `clauses`, `risk_findings`, `redlines`
5. Worker generates summary, updates `contracts.status = ready`, sends Resend email
6. Frontend polls `GET /contracts/:id` every 3s while processing, then renders review UI
7. User accepts/rejects redlines -> API updates DB -> Export job generates annotated DOCX/PDF to S3 -> Presigned GET URL for download

## 2. Database Schema

PostgreSQL via Prisma. All tables have `id uuid PK default gen_random_uuid()`, `created_at timestamptz`, `updated_at timestamptz` unless noted.

- **organizations:** `name text`, `slug text unique`, `plan text default 'trial'` [trial/pro], `stripe_customer_id text nullable`
- **users:** `clerk_user_id text unique`, `email text unique`, `full_name text`, `avatar_url text nullable`
- **organization_members:** `organization_id FK`, `user_id FK`, `role text` [owner/admin/member/viewer], unique(`organization_id`,`user_id`)
- **playbooks:** `organization_id FK`, `name text`, `description text`, `is_default boolean`, `rules jsonb` - array of {clause_type, acceptable_position, fallback_position, unacceptable_position, risk_if_missing}
- **contracts:** `organization_id FK`, `uploaded_by FK users`, `playbook_id FK`, `title text`, `original_filename text`, `file_type text` [pdf/docx], `s3_key text`, `file_size_bytes int`, `page_count int nullable`, `status text` [uploaded/processing/ready/failed], `overall_risk_score int` 0-100, `summary text nullable`, `executive_summary jsonb nullable` {key_dates, parties, total_value, top_risks[]}
- **contract_text_blocks:** `contract_id FK`, `page_number int`, `block_index int`, `text text`, `bbox jsonb nullable` - for PDF highlighting later, MVP can be null for DOCX
- **clauses:** `contract_id FK`, `clause_index int`, `clause_type text` [indemnification, limitation_of_liability, termination, confidentiality, ip_ownership, payment_terms, governing_law, auto_renewal, non_compete, data_protection, other], `title text`, `original_text text`, `start_block_id FK`, `end_block_id FK`, `page_start int`, `page_end int`
- **risk_findings:** `contract_id FK`, `clause_id FK nullable` (null = missing clause), `risk_level text` [critical/high/medium/low/none], `category text`, `explanation text`, `playbook_deviation text`, `confidence float` 0-1
- **redlines:** `clause_id FK unique`, `suggested_text text`, `rationale text`, `diff_html text nullable`, `status text default 'pending'` [pending/accepted/rejected/modified], `decided_by FK users nullable`, `decided_at timestamptz nullable`
- **reports:** `contract_id FK`, `generated_by FK`, `s3_key_pdf text`, `s3_key_docx text`, `version int`
- **processing_jobs:** `contract_id FK`, `job_type text` [process/export], `status text` [queued/running/succeeded/failed], `attempts int default 0`, `error_message text nullable`, `started_at`, `finished_at`
- **audit_logs:** `organization_id FK`, `user_id FK`, `action text`, `entity_type text`, `entity_id uuid`, `metadata jsonb`, `ip_address text`

Indexes: `contracts(organization_id, status, created_at desc)`, `clauses(contract_id, clause_index)`, `risk_findings(contract_id, risk_level)`, all FKs indexed.

## 3. Backend API Endpoints

Base: `/api/v1`, all except webhooks require Clerk JWT. All responses `{ data: ..., error: null }` or `{ data: null, error: { code, message } }`.

- `POST /contracts/upload-url` - Req: `{ filename: "MSA.pdf", fileType: "application/pdf", playbookId: "uuid" }` Res: `{ contractId: "uuid", uploadUrl: "https://s3...", s3Key: "org123/contract456/original.pdf" }`
- `POST /contracts/:id/complete` - Req: `{ fileSizeBytes: 284392 }` Res: `{ id: "uuid", status: "processing", jobId: "uuid" }`
- `GET /contracts?status=ready&search=acme&page=1&limit=20` - Res: `{ items: [{ id, title, status, overallRiskScore, pageCount, createdAt, uploadedBy: { name } }], total: 42 }`
- `GET /contracts/:id` - Res: `{ id, title, status, summary, executiveSummary: { parties: ["Acme Inc","Vendor LLC"], effectiveDate: "2026-01-01", totalValue: "$120,000/yr", topRisks: ["Unlimited liability"] }, overallRiskScore: 78 }`
- `GET /contracts/:id/clauses` - Res: `{ items: [{ id, clauseType: "limitation_of_liability", title: "Limitation of Liability", originalText: "...", pageStart: 4, risk: { level: "high", explanation: "No cap on liability", confidence: 0.92 }, redline: { id, suggestedText: "...", rationale: "...", status: "pending" } }] }`
- `PATCH /redlines/:id` - Req: `{ status: "accepted" }` or `{ status: "modified", suggestedText: "edited text..." }` Res: `{ id, status, decidedAt }`
- `POST /contracts/:id/export` - Req: `{ format: "docx", includeSummary: true }` Res: `{ reportId: "uuid", status: "processing" }`, poll `GET /reports/:id` for `{ downloadUrl }`
- `GET /contracts/:id/report` - Returns summary data for in-app report view, same shape as executiveSummary + clause counts by risk
- `GET /playbooks` / `POST /playbooks` / `PATCH /playbooks/:id` / `DELETE /playbooks/:id` - POST Req: `{ name: "Our Standard MSA Playbook", rules: [{ clauseType: "limitation_of_liability", acceptablePosition: "Cap at 12 months fees", fallbackPosition: "Cap at 2x annual fees", unacceptablePosition: "Unlimited liability" }] }`
- `GET /organizations/me/members` / `POST /organizations/me/invites` - Req invite: `{ email: "lawyer@firm.com", role: "member" }`
- `POST /webhooks/clerk` - Syncs user/org creation from Clerk, verified with Svix signature
- `GET /health` - Res: `{ status: "ok", db: true, redis: true }`

Validation: Zod schemas per route, file type allowlist pdf/docx only, max 25MB, max 100 pages.

## 4. Authentication and Authorization Strategy

- **Provider:** Clerk. Gives hosted login, Google + Microsoft SSO, email/password, org management, and invites in 1 day vs building it. Alternative considered Auth0 - Clerk is faster for B2B orgs in Next.js.
- **Flow:** Clerk issues JWT -> Next.js middleware protects routes -> Frontend sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>` -> Fastify verifies with `@clerk/fastify` / Clerk JWKS, extracts `userId` and `orgId`.
- **Sync:** Clerk webhook creates mirrors in `users`, `organizations`, `organization_members`. DB is source of truth for roles.
- **Authorization:** Middleware `requireOrgMember(req)` on every contract route, `requireRole(['owner','admin'])` for playbook delete, member invites, billing. Every query scoped: `where: { organizationId: req.orgId }` - never trust client-supplied orgId.
- **Roles:** Owner = billing + delete org, Admin = manage members/playbooks, Member = upload/review/export, Viewer = read-only contracts/reports, cannot see redline accept/reject buttons (enforced API + UI).
- **File security:** S3 bucket private, presigned URLs only, keys prefixed by organizationId, API checks ownership before issuing GET URL. Virus scan: worker runs ClamAV `clamscan` on download before parsing, fails job if infected.

## 5. Frontend Key Screens and Navigation

Framework: Next.js 14, Tailwind, shadcn/ui components, TanStack Query for data fetching, Zustand for review-page local state.

Layout: Left sidebar (collapsible) + top bar with org switcher (Clerk OrganizationSwitcher), user menu, search.

Sidebar navigation:
- Dashboard
- Contracts
- Playbooks
- Reports
- Team Settings
- Billing (placeholder Stripe link)

Screens:
- **/sign-in, /sign-up:** Clerk hosted components embedded
- **/dashboard:** Stats cards (contracts reviewed this month, avg risk score, critical findings open), recent contracts table, upload CTA
- **/contracts:** Filterable table - title, counterparty (from summary), risk badge, status, uploader, date. Search + status filter.
- **/contracts/new:** Drag-drop upload (react-dropzone), select playbook dropdown, progress bar to S3, redirect to processing screen
- **/contracts/:id/processing:** Stepper UI - Extracting text -> Identifying clauses -> Assessing risk -> Generating redlines, polled status, failure state with retry button
- **/contracts/:id/review - core screen:** 3-pane layout. Left: clause list grouped by risk, filter chips. Center: original contract text viewer (rendered text blocks with clause highlighting, page numbers - not full PDF renderer in MVP). Right: selected clause detail - risk explanation, playbook position, redline diff view (using `diff` npm package, red/green), Accept / Reject / Edit buttons, rationale.
- **/contracts/:id/report:** Executive summary, parties/key dates/value table, risk heatmap by clause type, findings table, Export PDF/DOCX buttons
- **/playbooks:** List + editor form with repeatable rule rows per clause type. Ship with 1 pre-seeded default playbook so users get value without configuring.
- **/settings/team:** Member list, invite form, role dropdowns

## 6. AI/LLM Pipeline for Clause Extraction, Risk Classification, and Redline Generation

Worker pipeline in Python, OpenAI Python SDK, Pydantic for structured output validation. No LangChain - direct calls are faster to debug in 7 days.

Step 1 - Extraction:
- PDF: `pdfplumber` for text + page numbers, fallback `PyMuPDF (fitz)` if pdfplumber returns <100 chars (scanned PDF -> mark failed, OCR is out of scope, tell user)
- DOCX: `python-docx` paragraphs + tables flattened to text
- Output: ordered text blocks with page numbers, joined full text capped at 200k chars

Step 2 - Clause segmentation:
- First pass regex/heading detection (numbered headings like `12. Indemnification`)
- Second pass: GPT-4o-mini with full text in chunks of 12k tokens with 500 token overlap, prompt returns JSON array of `{title, clause_type, start_quote, end_quote}`. We map quotes back to text via fuzzy search (`rapidfuzz`) to get offsets/pages. If mapping fails, keep clause with full chunk text.
- Dedupe overlapping clauses by index.

Step 3 - Risk classification per clause (parallel, max 10 concurrent calls):
- Model: GPT-4o-mini, temperature 0.1, Structured Outputs JSON schema: `{ risk_level, category, explanation, playbook_deviation, confidence }`
- Prompt includes: clause text, clause_type, org playbook rule for that type, instruction to be conservative and quote specific problematic language.
- Also run a missing-clause check: 1 GPT-4o-mini call with list of found clause_types vs expected 10 types, returns missing types -> create risk_findings with clause_id null, risk based on playbook.

Step 4 - Redline generation (only for critical/high/medium):
- Model: GPT-4o, temperature 0.2. Prompt: original clause + playbook acceptable/fallback position + risk explanation -> return `{ suggested_text, rationale }`. Instruction: minimal edit, preserve defined terms, numbers, party names.
- Generate word diff server-side with Python `difflib` -> store HTML for frontend.

Step 5 - Summary:
- Model: GPT-4o, 1 call with all clause summaries + findings (not full contract, saves tokens). Returns structured JSON: parties, effective date, term, total value, key dates, top 5 risks, overall assessment. Compute `overall_risk_score` deterministically in code: critical=25pts, high=15, medium=7, low=2, capped 100 - do not let LLM invent the score.

Reliability: Each LLM call wrapped with `tenacity` retry 3x exponential backoff on 429/5xx, 60s timeout, Pydantic validation retry once with error fed back. If a clause fails after retries, mark confidence 0 and continue - never fail whole contract for 1 clause. Log prompt version `v1` with every finding for debugging.

Cost control: GPT-4o-mini for 80% of calls, GPT-4o only for redlines/summary. Cache playbook text in prompt, truncate clauses to 4000 chars.

Local dev: Docker Compose with Postgres, Redis, MinIO (S3 mock), `pnpm dev` + `python worker.py`.

## 8. Observability, Logging, and Error Handling

- **Error tracking:** Sentry - `@sentry/nextjs`, `@sentry/node`, `sentry-sdk` Python. Every API 5xx and worker failure captured with contractId/jobId tags, no contract text in Sentry payloads.
- **Logging:** API uses `pino` JSON structured logs, Worker uses Python `structlog`. Log fields: `request_id` (UUID per request, propagated to job), `organization_id`, `user_id`, `contract_id`, `job_id`, `duration_ms`. Shipped to Axiom via Fly log shipper / Vercel log drain.
- **Product analytics:** PostHog - track upload_started, processing_completed, redline_accepted, report_exported. No document content sent.
- **Uptime/health:** Fly health checks on `/health`, Better Uptime pinging API + web every 5 min, alert to Slack/email.
- **LLM observability:** Log per call to DB table in metadata: model, prompt_version, input_tokens, output_tokens, latency, cost estimate. Dashboard query in Supabase to watch cost per contract. Alert if avg cost/contract > $0.75.
- **Error handling UX:** API returns typed error codes `FILE_TOO_LARGE`, `UNSUPPORTED_FILE`, `PROCESSING_FAILED`, `LLM_UNAVAILABLE`. Frontend shows human message + Retry button for processing failures. Worker jobs: max 3 attempts, then `status=failed`, user emailed, admin Slack alert via webhook.
- **Audit:** All uploads, exports, redline decisions written to `audit_logs` - critical for legal customers.

Daily rhythm: 15-min standup, end-of-day integration merge - no feature branches living >1 day.

## 10. Cost Estimate for Infrastructure and AI Usage at 100 Active Users/Month

Assumptions: 100 users, 20 contracts/user/month = 2,000 contracts/month, avg 12 pages / 8,000 words / ~30 clauses per contract.

Infrastructure:
- Vercel Pro: $20/month
- Supabase Pro: $25/month
- Fly.io API (2x 512MB) + Worker (2x 1GB): $35-55/month
- Upstash Redis: $10-20/month
- AWS S3 (~200GB with exports) + requests: $8/month
- Resend (3k emails free tier, then): $0-20/month
- Sentry Team: $26/month
- Axiom + PostHog free tiers: $0/month
- Domain/Cloudflare: $2/month
- **Infrastructure subtotal: $126-176/month**

AI usage per contract:
- Clause segmentation: ~35k input / 3k output tokens on GPT-4o-mini = ~$0.008
- Risk classification: 30 clauses x (800 in / 150 out) GPT-4o-mini = ~$0.006
- Missing clause + summary: GPT-4o ~4k in / 800 out = ~$0.055
- Redlines: avg 8 clauses needing redlines x (900 in / 400 out) GPT-4o = ~$0.14
- **Per contract: ~$0.21, at 2,000 contracts: ~$420/month**

**Total estimated: $550-600/month, ~$5.50-6.00 per active user/month.** Charge $49-99/user/month and margin is healthy. Biggest lever is redline count - cap GPT-4o redlines to top 10 findings per contract in MVP.

## 11. Top 5 Technical Risks and Specific Mitigations

- **Risk 1 - LLM hallucinates risks or invents clause language, lawyers lose trust / liability:** Mitigation - temperature 0.1-0.2, structured outputs only, every finding must reference original clause text stored from extraction (never LLM-rewritten original), confidence scores shown, deterministic risk score in code, prominent "not legal advice" disclaimer, human accept/reject required for every redline. Log prompt version to reproduce issues.
- **Risk 2 - Confidential contracts leak or cross-tenant access - existential for legal:** Mitigation - private S3 with org-prefixed keys, presigned URLs only, every API query org-scoped and tested Day 5, encryption at rest SSE-KMS + TLS, OpenAI API with zero data retention request / confirm DPA terms and state in privacy page that data is not used for training via API, auto-delete original files option (30-day lifecycle for exports), audit logs. Do not log contract text in Sentry/Axiom.
- **Risk 3 - PDF parsing fails on scanned, complex, or table-heavy contracts:** Mitigation - dual parser fallback pdfplumber -> PyMuPDF, minimum text threshold check that fails gracefully with clear user message, test corpus of 15 real-world formats on Day 3/5, DOCX encouraged in UI. OCR with AWS Textract is fast-follow, explicitly not promised Day 7.
- **Risk 4 - Processing is slow or OpenAI rate limits kill throughput:** Mitigation - async queue architecture from Day 1 (never process in API request), parallel clause calls capped at 10 concurrent, GPT-4o-mini for bulk work, tenacity retries with backoff, show progress stepper so 60-120s wait feels intentional, Fly worker can scale to 4 instances in minutes. Target p95 < 2 min for 15-page contract.
- **Risk 5 - DOCX redline export does not look like real Word tracked changes, lawyers reject it:** Mitigation - do not fake tracked changes in MVP. Export is annotated DOCX: original clause, comment bubble with risk + rationale, suggested replacement in separate section + clean summary PDF. Set expectation in UI copy "Annotated export" not "Tracked changes". Real OOXML tracked-changes XML generation is post-MVP once validated users want it.

## 12. What Is Explicitly Out of MVP Scope

- Real Word tracked-changes (redline in-place with OOXML revisions) - annotated export only
- OCR for scanned/image PDFs, handwriting, non-English contracts
- E-signature, negotiation/counterparty collaboration, email sending to counterparty
- Contract lifecycle management: renewals, reminders, repository search across all contracts, obligation tracking
- Integrations: Salesforce, HubSpot, DocuSign, Ironclad, Slack, Google Drive/SharePoint sync
- Custom ML model training/fine-tuning, custom clause library training on customer data
- Real-time collaborative editing, comments/mentions, version comparison between two contract drafts
- Billing automation - Stripe checkout is a placeholder link/manual invoicing for design partners (add Stripe in week 2)
- Mobile app and full mobile review experience - desktop-first, mobile is read-only
- SOC 2, HIPAA, formal pen test - we follow best practices and document them, certification is post-MVP
- Bulk upload (more than 1 file at a time), API access for customers, webhooks for customers
- Re-running analysis on same contract after playbook change - user re-uploads in MVP
